Since the couple returned to the United Kingdom, their search for a new home in Britain has been a hotly debated topic, especially in light of their disagreements with the royal family and security concerns. The mystery surrounding their residence has fueled speculation and various theories. Where would the Sussexes choose to settle? That was the question echoing everywhere on social media and in the press. For security reasons, the details of their living arrangements have always remained confidential.

As reported by the British media, the couple and their two children had been staying at a property owned by a wealthy friend, nestled in the Cotswolds countryside—an area Harry and Meghan already knew well. In 2018, the year of their wedding, they rented a prestigious farmhouse in the region for two years—a historic property with an estimated value of 4.12 million British pounds (about $5.5 million), part of the Great Tew Estate. The residence included a four-bedroom farmhouse, a barn converted into living quarters, and a separate cottage with two additional bedrooms. The property also featured extensive grounds and a heated patio. Over the years, the Cotswolds, in the English countryside, have become a retreat for numerous celebrities, including Jeremy Clarkson, David and Victoria Beckham, and Kate Moss. A few weeks ago the Duchess of Sussex was photographed at The Three Horseshoes, a quaint pub near Burford, in the company of Ellen DeGeneres and her wife, Portia de Rossi. In 2024, DeGeneres and de Rossi left the United States to move to the Cotswolds, where they live on a large estate surrounded by greenery.

The Sussexes’ housing history in the United Kingdom, however, has been quite eventful. Before leaving the United Kingdom, the couple lived at Frogmore Cottage in Windsor, a property made available to Harry and Meghan by Queen Elizabeth II. In 2023, however, the two royals left the residence. The decision came a few months after the publication of the duke’s memoir, Spare. To renovate Frogmore Cottage, approximately 2.4 million British pounds (about $3.2 million) went into transforming two existing buildings into a single-family home. The renovations were extensive: The ceiling beams and floor structures were replaced, the electrical system was redone, new gas and water lines were installed, and a soundproofing system costing approximately 50,000 British pounds (about $67,000) was reportedly put in place. Despite the significant spend, the Sussexes left the property for good after moving overseas.

Even before settling in Windsor, Harry and Meghan lived at Nottingham Cottage, within the Kensington Palace complex. It was a rather small residence that apparently hadn’t won Meghan over. In the Netflix documentary Harry & Meghan, the duchess recalled with a touch of irony that the name Kensington Palace suggested something grand, while the reality was quite different: “Kensington Palace sounds very regal, of course it does. His private life has been marked by tragedy: In 1994 he lost his first wife, Joanna, and their two young children in a car accident in Hampshire.

However, being hosted by a wealthy friend is nothing new in the Sussexes’ lives. In 2020, when they decided to step back from their royal duties and move to the United States, the couple stayed at the Beverly Hills mansion of producer and media mogul Tyler Perry. The property is located within the CostaTerra Golf & Ocean Club, an exclusive residential complex with about 300 ocean-view villas in Melides, south of Lisbon.

Meanwhile, the Duke and Duchess of Sussex are expected in Brussels on November 10 for an event dedicated to protecting children from online risks and abuse. The heart of the initiative, organized by MEP Antonio López-Istúriz White as part of a parliamentary intergroup, will be the unveiling of The Lost Screen Memorial, a video installation created in memory of children who lost their lives after falling victim to online abuse and exploitation. According to reports in the British media, Harry and Meghan will deliver a joint speech on the issue—which has long been a focus of the couple’s advocacy—before participating in a discussion with international activists. Another discovery reportedly took place in recent days at a storage unit that Thomas Markle allegedly rented near his former home in Rosarito, Mexico. The facility was reportedly inspected by local police as part of an investigative operation. Meghan’s 82-year-old father has reportedly been transferred in recent days to a facility in Florida that specializes in caring for people with dementia, according to The Sun.

His move to a care facility could now complicate the investigation, particularly the possibility of questioning Thomas Markle. His cognitive condition could make it more difficult to proceed with the investigation, especially given the protections afforded to residents of specialized facilities.

Meghan, who has had no contact with her father since 2018, has not commented on the latest developments. It had previously emerged that the duchess, who had been aware of the allegations against her father since 2018, wanted to speak out publicly. One of the agents from Royalty and Specialist Protection (RaSP)—the Scotland Yard unit responsible for the security of members of the royal family and other public figures—reportedly advised her not to speak out. Thomas Markle was arrested in Florida on Friday on charges connected to the possession of child sexual abuse material. He has previously denied possession of such material.

#3629. Celebrity Accused of Misconduct Is Named After Attempt to Hide Identity

British comedian David Walliams has been accused of sexual misconduct after previously attempting to conceal his identity.

Walliams, a children’s book author and judge on Britain’s Got Talent, was officially named in a report by The Guardian on Tuesday, November 10. According to the outlet, multiple women accused Walliams, now 55, of using his status to groom them. Two of the accusers, who are now in their 30s, were allegedly 15 when they met Walliams.

The allegations reportedly span decades. Walliams was identified following a lengthy investigation by The Guardian and ITV News.

Walliams previously sought an injunction against the media companies in order to prevent his name from being released, with his lawyers claiming he was a suicide risk. The request was denied by a judge earlier this month.

Last year, Walliams’ entire back catalog of published works was dropped by HarperCollins following an internal investigation over “inappropriate behavior” toward female employees. The Guardian alleged Walliams had a sexual relationship with a junior member of staff at the publishing company.

Walliams denied the accusations against him in a statement published Tuesday.

“Looking back, I realize that at times I behaved thoughtlessly towards other people I had casual sexual relationships with,” he began. “I realize I did not always take people’s feelings properly into account. That is something I regret. And whilst a power imbalance is inevitable when one party is famous, abusing that power is something else entirely and it is something I never did.”

Walliams insisted, “I am not a sexual predator. I have not broken the law, but I am devastated that some of the women I met 10 to 20 years ago have now expressed hurt or anger towards me.”

During court proceedings earlier this month, Walliams’ attorney, Sara Mansoori KC, noted he had “been hospitalized for months” and “has no intention of returning to public life” amid the ongoing scandal.

The attorney representing the media organizations involved in the case, meanwhile, argued Walliams’ alleged victims were also “traumatized” by his behavior and “have suffered mental health crises” of their own. The lawyer further argued “the obligation falls on the hospital” to keep Walliams safe and his mental health is not the responsibility of the media outlets.

#3628. Death Stranding 2 Headlines PlayStation Plus Game Catalog For November

The next batch of games for the PlayStation Plus Game Catalog has been revealed. PS Plus Essential and Premium subscribers can grab 10 games in total this month, starting November 11. In the US and UK, several of these games will roll out later in the month.

This month's headline act is Death Stranding 2: On the Beach, a post-apocalyptic open-world game from the mind of Hideo Kojima. A game about human connection at its core, Death Stranding 2 is a polarizing and delightfully weird game, so if the idea of GTA 6's bustling metropolis doesn't appeal to you, then maybe delivering packages in a desolate Australian landscape might appeal to you.

Or if you want the hustle and bustle of a sandbox without the consequences GTA 6 is teasing, Like a Dragon: Pirate Yakuza in Hawaii is worth checking out. This spin-off features fan-favorite character Majima as the protagonist, and as you'd expect from a Yakuza game, it's downright strange, melodramatic, and action-packed.

Other highlights this month include the Dragon Quest 3 HD-2D Remake for a modernized spin on a JRPG classic, survival-action meets the irradiated British countryside in Atomfall, and Trepang 2 is a blistering blast of first-person action.

The hardcore World War 2 first-person shooter Hell Let Loose features massive multiplayer battles, and if you're feeling sporty, you can attempt to hit a six in Cricket 2026 or taunt gravity with some exceptionally tight cornering in MotoGP 26.

PlayStation Plus Premium subscribers can also add two classics to their library: Soul Reaver 2 and Freedom Wars Remastered.

PlayStation Plus Game Catalog for November 2026

  • Death Stranding 2: On the Beach (PS5)
  • Like a Dragon: Pirate Yakuza in Hawaii (PS5, PS4)
  • Atomfall (PS5, PS4)
  • Dragon Quest 3 HD-2D Remake (PS5)
  • Trepang 2 (PS5)
  • MotoGP 26 (PS5)
  • Hell Let Loose (PS5)
  • Cricket 2026 (PS5, PS4)
  • Soul Reaver 2 (PS5, PS4) | PS Plus Premium required
  • Freedom Wars Remastered (PS5, PS4) | PS Plus Premium required

Sony says it'll also retire the PlayStation Plus app on PC on December 10. The company says fewer than 0.4% of subscribers used the app, so the PlayStation Plus cloud-streaming app on PC will no longer be available starting next month.

All PlayStation Plus subscribers can also grab a trio of freebies between now and November 30: Dead Island 2, Tomb Raider 4-6 Remastered, and Monster Train 2.

#3627. Vija Celmins, the Ultimate Artist’s Artist, Gets Honored by LACMA

On Wednesday, I walked down Crosby Street and stopped at an easy-to-miss building where, high above the cobblestoned street, is the studio of Vija Celmins, who’s been there for almost 50 years. It’s a classic gigantic SoHo artist loft, the kind you’ll be shocked to hear still exist—but they do. In the 1970s, the previous tenant put a Buddhist temple in the front room. Not finding anything particularly wrong with that, Celmins lived in the temple for a while.

“Then I finally thought, gee, maybe I could put a couch in here,” Celmins told me as I walked in.

Read True Colors: Inside the global deals and colorful critiques that make the art world go round, with a weekly guide to the must-see openings, auctions, and fairs.

It’s been decades since the galleries moved from SoHo to Chelsea and got replaced by boutiques. But among this warren of cast iron buildings, some of the artists who moved in during the pioneer days remain. Among them is Celmins, the masterful pop-landscapist who paints in infinite textures, taking on the universal with an obsessive tenacity. The 88-year-old is a living link to a long-gone generation, and someone always in the running when we talk about the best artists who are both still with us and who began their careers before the JFK assassination.

Approaching nonagenarian status, Celmins is still incredibly quick, with a generous, buoyant voice. She immediately hopped down the stairs of her old studio and took me over to the windows.

“I used to be able to see down the street before they built this ugly pink building—all the way to the bridge, because this was a parking lot,” she told me, referring to a building erected 21 years ago.

She walked past a print she made some years ago: a depiction of the ocean, her most famous subject, installed on the wall. She admired it in a refreshingly objective way.

“It’s so loose. Usually I tighten everything down,” she said. “I mean, it’s such a relief. I had forgotten that. And what did I do? I only made 10 of them, which is interesting, in ’16. I must have done this at… It looks like it’s a drypoint—doesn’t it look like drypoint? I mean, I did a fucking lot of oceans, as you know.”

Though not a household name, in certain circles, Celmins has attained near-mythic status. The very few people I told about this interview ahead of time were shocked she was having anyone over to her studios in Manhattan and Long Island. She works incredibly slowly, and thus has shown incredibly infrequently. This has started to change in the last few years. She had a retrospective at the Met Breuer in 2019, and in the last few years, a few shows of new work at her gallery, Matthew Marks—the blue-chip commercial concern that represents a disproportionate number of the greatest American artists.

Next year, Celmins will have a show at Dia Bridgehampton. Tomorrow, she’s the guest of honor at the LACMA Art+Film Gala, a big deal in American museumdom. It comes with a gigantic bash presided over by Leonardo DiCaprio and Eva Chow. The gala’s also honoring Denis Villeneuve, which Celmins is excited about. She’s seen the Dune movies and, like Villeneuve, is a big fan of the desert.

During my visit, she opened up a random drawer under a drawing table. There was stuff everywhere, decades of sketches and notes and Post-its. She has a constellation of postcards taped to the wall, with paintings as inspiration, ones that look nothing like Vija Celmins—Picasso, Balthus—along with photos of her heroes and her friends with pets. There’s Jasper Johns with his dog, Borges with his cat. She’s got framed artworks from friends who are mostly dead now, like a Ken Price drawing of some undulating cups—“You know Kenny Price?”—and a very kooky, absolutely amazing H.C. Westermann of a wolf with its heart throbbing in its chest, wandering through the desert. Westermann made it for her. She made Westermann a wolf drawing in return. She doesn’t know what happened to her wolf.

There are drawings of globes, sculptures of globes, her tablet paintings, more prints of the ocean, a paperweight from an insurance company in Kansas City—near where she grew up in Indiana after leaving Latvia—a wrapped-up canvas labeled “ED MOSES” on the side, and plenty of drawings of Saturn.

She moved into the SoHo place after two decades working in Venice Beach, California. While in LA, she honed and refined, and inarguably mastered, a painstakingly laborious practice of applying graphite to paper in slow, methodical marks, rendering the passage of time in hyperreal landscapes. She now mostly works in a studio on the eastern end of Long Island, where she's had a place for the last few decades. But it’s here at the SoHo studio, in the erstwhile cauldron of cutting-edge American art, where she loves to be.

“The studio out in the country is more like where I went back to painting, really,” she told me. “And here I did all these weird things.”

This wasn’t the first time we had met. A few weeks back, I was admiring the very cool Gary Hume show that Marks had up in his gallery on 24th Street when gallery director Jacqueline Tran tapped me on the shoulder and asked if I would like to meet Vija Celmins. Vija Celmins! At the public opening!

We chatted for a few moments. She seemed spry, fit, with an elastic mind. Then she invited me over for lunch—not in the city, but at her place on farmland out east. On an October morning I hopped on a Jitney, then an Uber to Celmins’s part of the hamlet, which is essentially rural, with small clapboard homes encircled by crop formations.

I arrived at the same time as my fellow visitors: Michael Govan, the director of LACMA, and his wife, the fashion executive Katherine Ross. Celmins welcomed us in and introduced us to her cat, Raymond, who immediately pounced on my cup of takeout coffee.

“Down, Raymond! He’s very friendly,” Celmins said. “He’s my son.”

Out here, in the two-room studio attached to her house, she’s been able to conjure a vision of landscape perhaps more potent than the breakthroughs she came to so many years ago. In her studio, she showed us how the raindrops on her window, as captured in her work-intensive flattened plane panorama, could take on epic qualities.

We sat down for lunch—quiche and soup from a local bakery—and Celmins started telling stories about California. She hadn’t lived there in a number of years, though the topography of the state is what willed her artwork into being. She drove out to the desert with James Turrell, with Doug Wheeler, and spent years—decades—arguing with Robert Irwin, who taught her at UCLA. Irwin called Celmins his “star student.” I’ve always liked this Bob Irwin quote about Celmins: “Vija has perfect taste. She doesn’t like anything.”

Govan told her about the museum, LACMA, and the new building that had finally been completed earlier this year after two decades of planning and fundraising. Celmins was quite curious about it all. She has a few plans for when she’s in town for the LACMA gala. She seemed intrigued about meeting her fellow honoree, director Villeneuve, and watched the Dune movies in preparation. (I heartily recommended she watch Sicario and Arrival as well.) She’s going to visit her old studio at 701 Venice Boulevard, which she hasn’t seen in decades.

“I was going to go out in the desert, but I’m not going to have time to do it,” she said. “I might have to make another trip. I really like the Death Valley desert because it’s so vast, so terrific. And they have airplanes zooming from the Air Force around really fast. I used to wave at them. They go really low, and they just go like, vvvvvrrroooooom! Right above, following the outline of the mountains.”

She’s also going to see Riko Mizuno, her Los Angeles art dealer, who is currently 94 years old. But most of her friends are gone.

“A lot of them have died, I mean, I didn’t have that many friends, but some died, and some are dying right now,” she said. “And then they moved away. Ed Moses, I knew pretty well. Billy Al Bengston. Well, Kenny Price, I loved Kenny.”

Then she mentioned Robert Therrien—“You know Bob Therrien?”—the late artist who has become quite famous for oversized sculptures that are astronomically popular on Instagram. A retrospective at The Broad this year became something of a sensation. I can’t imagine an artist more different than Celmins—but as it turns out, they had a deep mutual respect for each other.

“I met him once, and he was a very unusual person,” Celmins said. “He was really tall, and everything in his studio was like—he had a ceiling that was maybe like 25, 28 feet tall. And he had this little ladder that went up this side to this kitchen, which was this kitchen he remade from Chicago or someplace where his family used to live. I’ll show you one little thing. He gave me this.”

She got up from her chair and found the Therrian artwork on a shelf. It was a snout, bobbing up and down in a terrifying manner, attached to a curved metal rod. Just the inner part of the face of a canine, floating forever.

“It’s so disorienting. Where’s the rest of the dog?” I asked.

#3626. GTA 6 Has Sold Almost 10 Million Copies So Far, And PS5 Is Massively Outselling Xbox (Of Course)

The video game research company Sensor Tower has updated its GTA 6 sales tracker to reveal the latest, albeit unofficial, sales data for the open-world crime game. According to Sensor Tower, GTA 6 has now sold 9.69 million total units via pre-purchases, which works out to about $942 million in gross revenue.

The report said PS5 sales are dominating the mix, with GTA 6 selling 7.23 million units on PS5 so far, compared to 2.46 million on Xbox Series X|S. That means of the 9.69 million GTA 6 sales so far, 75% are on PS5 and 25% on Xbox Series X|S.

In total, GTA 6 sales for PS5 have so far reached $703 million in revenue, compared to $239 million for Xbox Series X|S. Sony and Microsoft keep about 30% of revenue due to their platform fees, so GTA 6 being a huge success directly benefits both of those companies.

The huge gap in sales between platforms is not surprising because the PS5 is dominating Xbox Series X|S in terms of console sales. In fact, GTA 6 is breaking records on Xbox, Microsoft has said, and the sales numbers for GTA 6 on Xbox line up with Xbox's share of the console market.

Sensor Tower is projecting as many as 25 million total pre-purchases for GTA 6 by launch, and if the 75/25 split holds, that would be about 18.5 million units on PS5 and 6.5 million on Xbox Series X|S.

GTA 6 is the most preordered game of all time for PlayStation and Xbox. If the 10 million pre-purchase number is real, that would break a record for most preorders set by Cyberpunk 2077 (8 million).

Sony holds the marketing rights for GTA 6 on PS5, but that doesn't mean that Microsoft is doing nothing to try to promote the game. Just recently, Microsoft announced a GTA 6-inspired custom Xbox console that sits inside an alligator.

Circana has released new data that shows that GTA 6 holds 29% purchase intent among US console and PC gamers. That means nearly 1 in 3 console and PC gamers in the US plan to buy GTA 6–this is the highest purchase intent that Circana has ever measured for any game.

GTA 6 may indeed be a gigantic hit commercially, and one that helps lift the entire industry with increased sales of hardware and accessories. But anyone looking to buy a new console to play GTA 6 is set for major sticker shock, as consoles today are more expensive than ever. Not only that, but GTA 6 is not going to save the industry’s many serious and deep-rooted issues, experts believe.

GTA 6 launches on November 19 for PS5 and Xbox Series X|S. The game's file size is about 212GB, and thankfully, preloading is already underway. The game unlocks on November 19 at midnight local time, and that means US players will be among the last in the world to get in.

People in New Zealand, meanwhile, will be the first in the world to play GTA 6. If you're thinking about booking a flight to the land of Hobbits, here are some tips for packing your PS5 safely.

#3625. Sadie Robertson Says Marriage 'Shifted' After Mom Noticed Their Struggles

Sadie Robertson and Christian Huff reexamined their marriage after her mother, Korie Robertson, pointed out noticeable relationship struggles post-baby.

“My mom wrote us a letter that was a loving letter of, ‘Here’s what I see you’re struggling with, and here’s what I think could help you,’” Sadie, 29, exclusively told Us while discussing her new memoir, It’s Not Personal: Coming Face-to-Face With Who You Really Are. “Those things are hard to receive. First of all, you’re dealing with embarrassment. You’re like, ‘Oh my gosh, like, this is so embarrassing. She sees I’m struggling.’”

Sadie revealed in her new book that Korie, 53, delivered her and Christian, 28, a note during a family trip to New York City to promote Duck Dynasty: The Revival. (At the time, Sadie was newly postpartum after welcoming her third daughter, Kit, in August 2025.)

In addition to feeling embarrassment over Korie’s letter, Sadie wondered why she and Christian were being singled out after six years of marriage.

“You’re like, ‘Is everybody else getting a letter? Oh, it’s just us. OK, shoot. You know, we really are doing rough,’” the “Whoa That’s Good” podcaster, who also shares daughters Honey and Haven with Christian, recalled. “That was such a confronting thing, but yeah, that was the thing that really shifted things for our relationship because we just got honest about it.”

Sadie continued, “I think so many times in life you, kind of, accept that this is just the way it’s gonna be, and yet a life of faith calls you higher than that. It goes, ‘That’s not the way it’s just gonna be. There’s something better for you.’ And my mom was saying, ‘Hey, like, I see this in y’all. It doesn’t have to be that way, you know?’”

For Sadie and Christian, Korie’s letter “meant so much” because of her empathic tone.

“She was like, ‘I remember when your dad and I were at that stage, and I remember how it felt to be going through that,’” Sadie told Us, referring to her father, Willie Robertson. “Immediately just that empathy made me go, ‘Tell me more.’”

Sadie revealed that Korie shared “really helpful” lessons that she said “helped them in their season of little kids and this many years married and whatnot.”

“I think Christian and I have just gotten to a point in our communication that we’re just so open and honest with each other,” Sadie noted. “We are quick to be able to say, ‘OK, I missed it there, or I was being selfish there, or I need to be more more kind even when I’m tired,’ or whatever it is, whatever the silly thing is, just saying it, being quick to apologize, being quick to change and turn the corner. It’s helped us so much in our marriage. I will say that letter really kickstarted it for us.”

Reaching the other side of their marital issues, Sadie further paid tribute to Christian by dedicating It’s Not Personal to him.

“Christian is truly just an incredible human,” she gushed to Us. “Christian really is the most incredible, encouraging human. He is my best friend, he is the best girl dad in the world, he is so incredible. I feel like he doesn’t need everybody to tell him how awesome he is, but I’m his wife and I get to. I just wanted to dedicate the book to him because, so much of this message, he’s helped teach me by living it.”

Just as Sadie learned helpful lessons from her husband and her mom, she similarly hopes to pass down those pearls of wisdom to readers.

“I hope people feel that way with my writing [as I did from my mom’s letter], that, like, I know how it feels,” she said. “I’m feeling that too, but here’s how I’m overcoming it.”

In It’s Not Personal, Sadie shares candid stories and biblical citations to help readers reclaim what should be “personal.”

“It’s called It’s Not Personal, and just the response to the title has been so awesome because people get it. Everyone knows when that is thrown out, ‘it’s not personal,’ it is personal,” she explained. “It’s always personal, it feels personal, and my angle with that was really just a draw for people who have been afraid to step into faith, who are afraid of the confrontation of getting to know God and what that looks like.”

It’s Not Personal: Coming Face-to-Face With Who You Really Are is out now.

Using AI as your assistant shopper before you take the plunge

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

It seems like in recent years, Black Friday sales happen a whole lot sooner than the actual day we all expect them to hit our timelines.

Instead of rushing out of the house as soon as it hits midnight while my Thanksgiving dinner is still digesting, I just have to keep an eye out for all the early online deals in the weeks leading up to that cost-effective holiday. The likes of Best Buy, Amazon, Walmart and Target are already posting up their biggest discounts, which have compelled me to set up an alert with Meta Muse whenever any ones geared toward video games go live.

But before I decide to go all-in on any Black Friday purchase, I’ve promised myself to tag in ChatGPT as my online shopping assistant to do a few things first. And with the following methods, fitting prompts and a bit of outside research, you’ll have a much easier time navigating the bargain-filled waters of Black Friday.

From choosing what’s actually worth purchasing to doing a final audit of everything you’re planning to buy, these are the best ways to use ChatGPT before you spend a single dime on Black Friday.

For the past couple of years, my Black Friday wishlist has been dominated by OLED TVs, gaming headsets, kitchen appliances (I’ve been in the market for a soda maker for far too long…) and anything else that requires it to be plugged in.

But once I actually look over that list and consider what’s worth adding to my already crowded bedroom that’s ruled by every piece of consumer tech you can think of, I start to wonder if I really need all of the items I’m hoping get a major Black Friday sale. ChatGPT can come in to help during this sort of conundrum by helping you decide what items on your wishlist are worth a purchase and which ones should be skipped entirely.

This prompt should make your final Black Friday purchasing decisions a lot easier to deal with:

Sign up to the Tom's AI Guide weekly newsletter summing up all the biggest AI news you need to know. Plus, analysis from our AI editors and tips on how to use the latest AI tools!

Here’s my Black Friday wishlist: [list of items]. My total budget is [dollar amount], and I already own [list of items]. Ask me [number] questions about what I actually need, then rank my list into buy, consider, and skip. Explain your reasoning.

Coming across a major price drop for something you’ve been eyeing for a good while hits all the right happiness sensors in my brain. But it’s always good to snap out of that optimistic mode and be more of a realist to see if that price is really that good of a deal.

ChatGPT can step in to check whether the advertised Black Friday sale price you’ve come across is really a steal or if that newly discounted price isn’t as great as it’s being marketed. Doing some price-drop digging with this prompt could propel you to look for a better deal on your most wanted Black Friday item:

This exact model [number or product link] is advertised at [dollar amount], supposedly down from [dollar amount]. Search for documented price history and previous sale prices. Is this unusually cheap or a routine discount? Cite dated sources and say what you couldn’t verify.

I’m prone to balling out on Black Friday, which is a bad habit I’m trying to leave in the past this year. To the point where I’m going to try to stay under $200 while I pick up the discounted items I really need. So, for the types of items that have the best practical uses in my kitchen and mancave, I’ll look up specific products I’ve been keeping a close eye on while also considering cheaper options that may fulfill the same uses as my wish-listed goods.

The following prompt is worth using if you’re approaching your future Black Friday sales from the same viewpoint:

I’m buying a [product name] for [list of specific uses], with a maximum budget of [dollar amount]. Identify my must-have specifications, then compare three suitable options. Include a cheaper or previous-generation alternative and explain what I would actually sacrifice.

For those items that require spending a whole lot more than just the initial entry price, it’s good to know what else you might be putting money toward when that item comes into your possession. Printers, coffee makers, video game consoles and mobile phones immediately come to mind as the products that reach into your pocket for additional charges. Subscriptions, required accessories, replacement parts, delivery and possible installation of said devices spring up as the type of charges I’m alluding to.

Putting the following ChatGPT prompt to good use during Black Friday should give you a clearer picture of everything you’ll possibly be paying for beyond the entry fee for whatever you’re considering buying:

Compare the first-year and three-year costs of these products: [links]. Include required accessories, subscriptions, replacement supplies, shipping, and installation where relevant. Separate optional extras from necessities and label estimates.

I love to go digging for product reviews on Reddit since I feel like the takes on there are usually pretty reliable. Anyone who takes the time out of their day to pen a 2000+-word review of their new SteelSeries Arctis Nova Pro gaming headset for free in a dedicated headphone subreddit has to be reliable, right? The same goes for folks who list out all the pros, cons and accompanying pics of whatever product they chose to say a few words about in the Amazon reviews section.

The following prompt should do you a lot of good when it’s time to see if the Black Friday item you’re planning to buy is highly rated or a total bust that comes with a serious cause of buyer’s remorse:

Research independent reviews and owner feedback for [exact model name or product link]. Identify recurring complaints, long-term reliability concerns, and the strongest positives. Distinguish measured test results from anecdotes, cite sources, and explain who should avoid this product.

There are those instances where you come across a price that may be a bit too good to be true once Black Friday sales start taking over your timeline. That highly discounted price may carry some factors that you may have never considered before, such as its actual seller (even if it’s being sold through a major online retailer), its condition (new or refurbished) and everything that comes with its return policy.

Putting the next prompt into ChatGPT should help you get a better understanding of what you’re planning to pick up and what catches (if any) may be attached to it:

Review this listing and its policies: [links or text]. Identify who sells and ships it, its condition, warranty coverage, return deadline, return shipping costs, restocking fees, and exclusions. Flag anything unclear that I should confirm before paying.

Before hitting that checkout button, it might be worth taking one last look at your digital cart full of Black Friday goodies and seeing if you need everything or could do without a few of them. Presenting your cart to ChatGPT and asking it to consider the biggest arguments against actually getting anything inside it is worth a shot. Sometimes you just need a second opinion to talk you out of buying yet another set of kitchen utensils or a blender just because it’s heavily discounted (and because you probably have one already and just want a new one).

Take this final prompt to ChatGPT and let it help you take a closer look at your Black Friday cart to reconsider what you’re buying:

Audit this cart: [items and prices]. My budget is [dollar amount], and my priorities are [priorities]. Make the strongest practical case against each purchase. Flag duplicate functions, compatibility issues, and unnecessary extras. Recommend a final cart within budget, allowing me to buy nothing.

We’re nowhere near Black Friday, but a whole slew of sales have begun littering everyone’s inboxes and timelines in the weeks ahead of that consumer-friendly holiday. With ChatGPT in your corner as a digital shopping assistant, you can use any of the aforementioned prompts to let it help you shop smarter.

Gather the evidence the chatbot has presented to you, do a bit of research of your own to check if its claims are factual and make your Black Friday purchasing decisions from there. Going the extra mile to use AI to help you comprehend what you’re considering buying on Black Friday is certainly worth doing this year and beyond, once you recognize how helpful it can be.

#3623. WoW: Forever Just Received Its First Big Post-Launch Changes

World of Warcraft: Forever received its first post-launch updates over the weekend, giving players a good reason to run each dungeon more than once alongside upcoming class tweaks.

On November 8, developer Blizzard issued a hotfix that increased kill experience while in dungeons by 50%. According to the forum post, Blizzard said this is so it "feels better to go back for more runs," and made reference to a Wailing Caverns dungeon quest to collect Deviate Hides that often requires more than one run.

It previously outlined upcoming class changes that will go live on November 10. Those changes will make it so Hunter and Warlock pets are sturdier, improve Affliction Warlock's damage-over-time spells, and make it so Enhancement Shamans will want to pursue strength and attack power items instead of intellect and spell power ones. 

The debate on how much experience dungeons should grant in Forever has been an ongoing back and forth since the game's beta. Initially, dungeons were particularly lucrative, with massive experience rewards from dungeon quests.

That changed about halfway through the beta due to concerns that players were leveling too quickly while doing dungeons. Blizzard axed dungeon quest experience as a result. While dungeons were still worthwhile to do once thanks to potent item rewards, doing them multiple times proved to be less valuable. With no quests to do, kill experience earned in dungeons was lackluster.

Forever's launch on November 4 carried that philosophy forward, but it quickly became apparent dungeons were simply not worth doing after one quest-focused run. It was even more of an issue considering that many dungeons have item-collection quests that are difficult to complete in a single run when all five members of the group are trying to do it at once. However, because doing a dungeon a second time was so inefficient when it came to earning experience, going back in to try and complete that quest felt like a waste of time. 

In an episode of the WoW: Forever podcast from October 8, Blizzard said it doesn't want dungeons to be a "one and done" experience while leveling, but also doesn't want them to be so rewarding that they become the most "efficient" way to level up. This latest tweak then seems to be Blizzard making good on that philosophy.

The class changes are smaller but still significant, particularly since Blizzard previously said not to expect major class changes prior to the arrival of Forever's endgame raids on December 9. They specifically address a key pain point for Enhancement Shamans, who have complained about their specialization's need for intellect and spell power gear despite being a melee-focused spec. Ahead of Forever's launch, the WoW Classic Shaman Discord shutdown in protest of the state of the class, and now Blizzard has made good on at least one of the Discord server's list of complaints. 

Forever's launch went surprisingly smooth, despite being the biggest concurrent-player launch in WoW's 22-year history. On the eve of launch, Blizzard revealed Forever's first new legendary weapon, Taldramir, the Whispering Wood.

#3622. Valve Is Giving You More Ways To Know If A Game Runs Well On Steam Deck

Valve's Steam Deck verification program has been a helpful, if somewhat flawed, method of determining if a game is a good fit for the company's handheld PC. But while many games might be granted a "Verified" badge, there have been many cases where real-world performance doesn't live up to the expectation of players. That's why Valve has introduced a more nuanced way for you to determine if a game is a good fit for the Steam Deck.

Along with the Steam Deck verification status, games will now feature average frame-rate data on the store page once Valve has gathered enough data from players. This will give you an indication of real-world performance on the Steam Deck, collecting data from other players using the Steam Deck in their default states and averaging it across their total playtime.

"The current Steam Deck Verified compatibility rating is based on standardized test criteria, but it may not match every customer’s bar for acceptable gameplay," the announcement post reads. "This is especially true around performance - a game with an Unsupported rating due to unstable performance may be considered playable by some customers, and a Verified game may not reach a framerate that some customers prefer to play at."

Alongside the average, Valve is also adding a histogram that let's you see numerous averages spread out over playtime. This can help you determine if a game has pockets of poor performance that might be dragging down the average, giving you even more information to help you determine if a purchase for Steam Deck play is worthwhile.

Valve relies on other players for this data. So while it says that thousands of games already have this featured on their store pages, there are still many more that require more playtime before they can be calculated and displayed. The data collection is opt-in, too, meaning only Steam users actively sharing their data through the Steam Beta Client will count towards these averages. Valve says it will be rolling out this program to the main Steam branch soon.

It also says that tools like this could come to other platforms in the future, but that it chose the Steam Deck first because of its standard hardware configuration. It's easy to see this being extended to the Steam Machine for the same reasons, with Valve potentially waiting for more of them to be in the hands of players before being able to accurately average the data. It's a useful metric that not only helps players make more informed buying decisions, but also potentially helps Valve determine what is, and isn't a meaningful jump in performance as it evaluates a potential Steam Deck successor.

#3621. How the Newly Elected Congress Can Save the Smithsonian

This is the November 6, 2026 edition of True Colors, a look inside the global deals and colorful critiques that make the art world go round, with a weekly guide to the must-see openings, auctions, and fairs.

It’s True Colors. The Democrats have flipped the House and the Senate, which could usher in a new era of funding at the Smithsonian—or, at the very least, a vibe shift in DC. There are a ton of gallery shows opening around New York, and on the West Coast, LACMA Art+Film Gala goes down tomorrow night. We got the rare chance to sit down with one of the night’s honorees, Vija Celmins.

Mentioned in this issue: Donald Trump, Lonnie Bunch, Alma Allen, Tilman Fertitta, Yoshitomo Nara, Loïc Gouzer, Vija Celmins, Matthew Marks, Leonardo DiCaprio, Eva Chow, Denis Villeneuve, Gary Hume, Jacqueline Tran, Michael Govan, Katherine Ross, James Turrell, Riko Mizuno, Matthew Barney, Roni Horn, Meshell Ndegeocello, Steve McQueen, Matthieu Blazy, Rosemarie Trockel, Carrie Mae Weems, Marina Abramović, Wade Guyton, Christopher Wool, Rashid Johnson, Felix Rödder, Calvin Marcus, James Ensor.

Trump has spent the last two years attacking Washington’s cultural hub with executive orders and legally dubious firings issued via fiat. But the Smithsonian gets its funding through Congress—what if Congress actually acted on that authority?

Sure, Congress has more pressing issues to address once the deeply blue House and Senate get sworn in early next year. But here at True Colors I think it’s fair to ask the question: Will lawmakers wind back the years of impact the Trump administration has had on the Smithsonian Institution?

Although Congress has authority over the cultural behemoth, the White House has in just the last two years issued executive orders, been extremely hands-on in its public signage, and mounted pressure campaigns to fire directors and censor artworks. Congress could have stopped all of this, but didn't. Republicans naturally didn’t want to cross Trump and support the beleaguered arts mecca. But Democrats have every reason to—after the new Congress is sworn in they’ll have the power to appropriate massive amounts of funding to each Smithsonian museum—or even create new museums. Plus, that can impact how the whole institution is run on a day-to-day basis, as Congress has the power to shake up the Smithsonian’s board of regents. That governing body will choose the next Smithsonian secretary, after Lonnie Bunch resigned earlier this year.

I’m particularly interested in who takes over as the director of the Hirshhorn Museum and Sculpture Garden. Melissa Chiu, who held the position for 12 years, stepped down earlier this year to be the director of the Guggenheim Museum in New York, and rumors are swirling about who will succeed her in the post. The prospect of a culture-living Congress—and, who knows...a Democratic president come 2029?—could make the Smithsonian seem like a swell place to be long term.

Add in the prospect of a new crop of congressional staffers and the attendant cottage industries of consultants and lobbyists all flocking to Washington, and I could see the Hirshhorn getting caught up in the vibe shift, pronto. There’s expected to be a sea change of DC residents in town, and there’s every reason to believe they’ll make the (free! always free!) contemporary art museum a constant stop on the rotation. Plus, the long-gestating renovation of the Sculpture Garden literally just opened this past weekend. I don’t have any inside intel on who’s in the running for the job —but it’s looking like a pretty great gig these days.

Read True Colors: Inside the global deals and colorful critiques that make the art world go round, with a weekly guide to the must-see openings, auctions, and fairs.

Meanwhile, the artworks that filled the American Pavilion at the Venice Biennale, made by State Department–tapped artist Alma Allen, might be stuck in Italy for the foreseeable future. Funding has run out, and there’s nothing in the budget for moving the works. I wonder how that can be resolved. Seems like a job for an art-loving, restaurant-owning Italian ambassador, Tilman Fertitta!

The massive two-location Yoshitomo Nara show opened at David Zwirner last night, truly one of the great gallery moments here in New York this season. Don’t miss the pop-up one-painting exhibition of Nara’s In the Milky Lake / Thinking One, which will be sold by Loïc Gouzer’s one-lot auction business, Fair Warning. It’s on view at 534 W. 22nd Street. The lot opens for live bidding November 19 and is expected to sell for the eye-popping sum of $10 million to $15 million.

You can also see Nara’s work in Washington, DC, where the aforementioned Hirshhorn just opened a grand survey of the artist timed to the inauguration of its sculpture garden. And if you want to check out some of Nara’s artworks in a very unexpected place, head to the Avenue A dive bar Niagara, where Nara drunkenly created a masterwork on the walls late one night after an opening at Pace. The bar wisely conserved the artwork behind glass, and it remains there nearly two decades later.

It’s not usually worth reporting on the toasts given at gala dinners here in the prized real estate that is this newspaper’s Table Hopping section, but the Dia Fall Night had some good honorary toast content! On Monday, Matthew Barney proved himself to be a very deep Roni Horn fan with his toast. Then Meshell Ndegeocello went super outside the box, honoring Steve McQueen by stepping in front of the podium and leading a band around the gala. The whole evening was like that. Chanel wasn’t just a sponsor—the brand’s creative director Matthieu Blazy, a true contemporary art head, chaired the whole thing alongside artists Rosemarie Trockel and Carrie Mae Weems. Marina Abramović was at my table; she told me she reads Vanity Fair every time she’s on a plane and appreciates how thick the issues have been lately. Marina, it’s an honor. Thank you for reading.

Matthew Marks hosted a party on Wednesday night for Wade Guyton’s excellent new show at Bridges, the best restaurant on Chatham Square. Fun fact: Christopher Wool’s old studio was right next to the restaurant some decades back.

On Election Day, as the results started coming in, Rashid Johnson opened a show of new work at Hauser & Wirth’s Wooster Street gallery, which has recently become my favorite of the mega-gallery’s dozen or so global outposts. It’s a throwback of sorts, a small space in the neighborhood that was once the city’s gallery nexus, with an excellent track record of great shows. The dinner was at the gallery’s restaurant, Manuela, right around the corner on Prince Street. There was caviar, and while it was served to celebrate Johnson, it happened to come out right as the news networks indicated the Democrats were going to flip a Senate seat in South Carolina. Spirits were high.

If you’re making your way to The Met to see “Krasner and Pollock: Past Continuous,” do stop by Rodder, the gallery founded by Felix Rödder, to see one of the most inspired artist pairings in the city right now. Calvin Marcus, the fanatically talented and free-wheeling Los Angeles painter, has new and recent paintings, drawings, and ceramics installed alongside work by the great Belgian weirdo James Ensor. The chemistry between these two artists from different centuries and continents is uncanny. The dinner for the show was held somewhere unusual: House of the Redeemer, the Episcopalian Church in a former Italian Renaissance Revival townhouse once owned by a Vanderbilt heiress.

#3620. Amid Higher Gas And Grocery Prices, GTA 6 Is A “Bargain” At $80, Take-Two CEO Says

It's no secret that life is expensive. Gas and grocery prices are up, in particular, and against that backdrop, Take-Two CEO Strauss Zelnick believes GTA 6 at $80 is a "bargain" due to how many hours people can play it.

"I think the consumer is under pressure. these are challenging times. Inflation has hit average consumers. Food prices are up. Gas prices are way up, and it's taking a toll," he told CNBC. "I think we are going to see that as we head into the Christmas season undoubtedly. Entertainment is not immune to such forces."

What gives Zelnick hope in this environment is that, in his belief, "interactive entertainment is actually a real bargain," and particularly a game like GTA.

"There are so many hours of engagement on offer. Even a short video game is 10 hours of engagement on the low end. You can play Grand Theft Auto 5 for hundreds of hours and not get bored. We'll see how people feel about Grand Theft Auto 6, but I believe that you'll be able to engage for an extraordinary long period of time," he said. "So if consumers look at entertainment value as the intersection of how great it is and how long you can engage with it, interactive entertainment is a great bargain. However, when you give people what they want, no matter what the times are, they will show up for it."

GTA 6's base edition costs $80, while there is also a $100 Ultimate Edition featuring a variety of additional in-game content. GTA 5, meanwhile, launched at $60 in 2013; that same $60 is about $85 today after adjusting for inflation. This is a point that Zelnick has made repeatedly when explaining why GTA 6 is actually a very good value. He's also said Rockstar could have charged even more for GTA 6, but chose not to so the game could reach more people.

While GTA 6's price is actually lower than what GTA 5 launched at in 2013, the same cannot be said for the hardware people need to play it on. The PS5 and Xbox Series X|S consoles are more expensive than ever due to the ongoing global component and memory shortages. If you're OK streaming the game, Microsoft just announced a 10-year deal with Take-Two that includes bringing GTA 6 to Xbox Cloud Gaming on the older Xbox One console.

GTA 6 launches on November 19 for PS5 and Xbox Series X|S, and preloading is now underway.

Megyn Kelly voiced her disapproval after Russell Brand was sentenced to over 10 years in prison for rape and sexual assault.

“I don’t believe the charges,” Kelly, 55, said during the Monday, November 9, episode of The Megyn Kelly Show. “And I don’t have to believe them just because the jury came through with the opposite conclusion. I feel indignant that this obvious conservative stalwart has been targeted.”

Brand, 51, received a sentence of 10 years and six months during a hearing on Monday, less than a week after he was found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault. (He was tried on a total of seven charges.)

“I’m good, I’m good,” Brand mouthed to his defense team after the ruling.

Multiple women accused Brand of sexual assault, rape and emotional abuse, with the allegations being explored in the Channel 4 documentary Russell Brand: In Plain Sight.

During her show on Monday, Kelly dismissed the claims made against Brand as “grabbing boobs, kissing, sniffing and having that kind of sex with a woman who consented to vaginal sex with him seconds beforehand, and also had clearly been joking with him.”

“And he had backdoor sex with a woman who licked his backdoor before she was even introduced to him,” she continued. “This is insane.”

Kelly argued the outcome of Brand’s trial was “an outrage,” adding, “This is an obvious double standard. And if you needed any further proof that this is a political witch hunt against Russell Brand, that judge just gave it to us.”

Brand previously denied the allegations ahead of his trial. His father, Ron Brand, also expressed his disappointment after the judge delivered the sentence on Monday, claiming his son was the “victim.”

Hours after the actor’s fate was revealed in court, news broke that he is under investigation for additional rape allegations made by two unidentified women.

There are a lot of upcoming Hallmark movies to look forward to, especially as Countdown to Christmas continues. Many of these films are led by Hallmark staples, of course, but it’s hard not to think about previous network stars who used to headline those offerings. This includes Danica McKellar, who is one of many ex-Hallmark stars to have joined rival company GAF. However, the Wonder Years alum is speaking out about the whole situation and wants fans to know she didn’t leave.

In 2021, McKellar exited Hallmark after signing a multi-picture deal with Great American Family. Over her six-year tenure at Hallmark, McKellar starred in nearly 20 films, so it was definitely a shock when her departure was confirmed. However, McKellar recently clarified the situation and made note of how Bill Abbott -- the former president and CEO of Hallmark Channel’s parent company, Crown Media -- factored into it. She told PauseRewind via Komo News:

I don't feel like I left. I feel like I stayed with the person and he has just given me so much more creative freedom.

Abbott was the president and CEO of Crown Media for 11 years before ultimately starting GAF. Considering their prior working relationship, it's admittedly understandable that McKellar would want to follow him to a new network. And, of course, the desire for more creative freedom is also reasonable for an actor.

So, from McKellar's point of view, she didn’t “leave” Hallmark but simply stuck with the person who helped build the network amid his venture into something new. As for how her new work situation is going, McKellar notes that she’s much more involved at GAF when it comes to making her movies. Overall, it sounds like the former child star has been relishing that:

I’m involved in rewrites for sure on the script. I help casting. I help make decisions about props. Sometimes I buy my own wardrobe or props because I'm like, oh, this would be perfect and they're always so receptive, which is great. And I'm very involved in the edit, choosing music, all that kind of stuff.

McKellar’s feelings about having creative control and being more involved are similar to what Candace Cameron Bure has said about GAF. The Full House alum, who also made the switch from Hallmark in 2022, has opened up about living her dream making faith-centered movies. She serves as an executive producer on all of her GAF films and even some films she doesn’t appear in. It definitely seems like both McKellar and Bure are a lot more hands-on than they were at Hallmark.

Even though McKellar is no longer on the network, she has no problem defending her Hallmark movies either. They’ve gotten a bad rap over the years, with many pointing out that Hallmark movies are far too predictable and the network hasn’t embraced POC and LGBTQ+-centric stories. However, the cable channel has been working to make some changes over the years, and McKellar still shows her support to her Hallmark friends and their movies.

While I miss seeing Danica McKellar on her previous network, I can’t say I blame her for being content at Great American Family. It's my hope that she continues to headline entertaining films that delight audiences whether they arrive during the holidays or not. On that note, though, with the holiday season coming up, there are going to be a lot more Christmas movies to look forward to that aren’t just on Hallmark.

#3616. How Elizabeth Taylor’s Childhood and Career Were Defined by Her Overbearing Mother

Elizabeth Taylor, like many other actors of her time, experienced the demands of Hollywood from a very young age. Her parents could never have imagined on February 27, 1932, just how much their newborn baby would achieve artistically. Sooner rather than later, however, they recognized her potential. Although she spent most of her life in Southern California in the heart of the movie industry, Taylor was born in Hampstead, England, to an American family consisting of her father, Francis Lenn Taylor, her mother, Sara Sothern, and their son, Howard, the movie star’s brother with whom she was close. They didn’t remain in Great Britain long, returning to the United States in 1939, shortly before World War II.

Sara Sothern with her children, Elizabeth and Howard Taylor.

The family sailed from London to New York and then settled in Los Angeles. By then, Taylor already had some experience in the performing arts, as she had been taking ballet lessons since she was just three years old. She made her debut in a recital that same year. Once in California, the father of the violet-eyed legend opened an art gallery featuring works imported from the UK. This would turn out to be an important step that brought the Taylors into the world of Hollywood. As biographer Alexander Walker would recount in Elizabeth: The Life of Elizabeth Taylor (Grove Press), the space “opened many doors for the Taylors, leading them directly into the society of money and prestige.”

Despite their differences, mother and daughter grew closer as they matured.

Sothern, the mother of this acting prodigy, saw her daughter as the perfect excuse to live the dream she didn’t fulfill because she was focused on caring for her family. If she couldn’t pursue an acting career, her daughter would. Seeing the effect that Taylor’s beauty had on others, Sothern set out to introduce her to people in the film industry. “Elizabeth Taylor probably wouldn’t have been an actress if it hadn’t been for her mother,” notes actor George Hamilton in the BBC documentary Elizabeth Taylor: Rebel Superstar. In this same documentary, Liz herself can be heard saying in an old recording: “My mother was an actress, but then she married my father, and he didn’t want her to be one, so she gave it up. I think she lived her life through me.”

Kate Andersen Brower, author of Elizabeth Taylor: The Grit and Glamour of an Icon (Harper Collins), explains that Sothern was behind the scenes trying to control every aspect of her daughter’s life in order to make her famous. This included sending Taylor to the same schools as the children of movie studio executives. Soon, thanks to a meeting with the fiancée of a high-ranking Universal Pictures exec who visited the gallery run by Taylor’s father, Elizabeth made her big-screen debut. Her early Hollywood years were propelled by connections her mother painstakingly built.

In 1949, Elizabeth Taylor and Sara Sothern pose at their home in Beverly Hills.

Taylor’s first movie was There’s One Born Every Minute, filmed when she was only 10 years old. Also starring Carl Switzer, who played Alfalfa in Our Gang, it was not a success, and Universal chose not to extend her option. Andersen Brower quotes the studio’s casting director: “The kid has nothing. Her eyes are too old; she doesn’t have the face of a kid.” Sara persisted, however, and through her husband, she met Sam Marx, a producer working on an MGM film, Lassie Come Home. Taylor would be cast in a small role.

Elizabeth Taylor and her mother in a 1948 photo taken in London.

Its success paved the way for another milestone in Taylor’s early career. At age 12, she landed the role of Velvet Brown in National Velvet, alongside Mickey Rooney and Angela Lansbury. Released in December 1944, it grossed almost $6 million worldwide, making it one of MGM’s top films of that period. Taylor signed a new contract with the studio, though she later complained about how she was treated by its head, Louis B. Mayer.

Elizabeth Taylor helps her mother prepare hot dogs and hamburgers at their home in Los Angeles in 1947.

At the same time, her father was both astonished by and jealous of his teenage daughter’s success. An alcoholic and physically abusive, on one occasion he punched her in the jaw, and for the rest of her life, she suffered from TMJ, or lockjaw. Andersen Brower writes, “She explained it away—as she always had—saying that her father was embarrassed that Taylor was the breadwinner of the family and that he felt emasculated.”

Sothern was a practicing Christian (though she was also interested in Judaism, which may have contributed to Taylor’s decision to convert to that religion so that she could marry Eddie Fisher, her fourth husband), and she taught her daughter from an early age that she could not sleep with any man until she was married to him. It’s a view that Taylor appears to have adopted: “Nothing comes off until the ring goes on,” she told gossip columnist Louella Parsons. Sothern, however, had her doubts. Before Taylor married Conrad “Nicky” Hilton in 1950, when she was just 18 years old, Sothern paid a doctor to confirm that her daughter was still a virgin and also to open her hymen to spare her pain during the first time she had sex.

Years later, Taylor would admit that her early years in the film industry were not easy. Her parents spent practically all the money she earned as a child actor. In a 1997 interview with Barbara Walters on 20/20, she described her childhood as “lonely.” She once confided to her close friend George Hamilton that she just wanted “to be a little girl again,” to relive those years that she never got to enjoy.

#3614. Sony Cancels Live-Service PS5 Game Fairgames, But No Layoffs

Sony has canceled the upcoming live-service shooter Fairgame$, but there will be no job cuts connected to the game's closure. This is according to a report from Bloomberg today.

The game was in the works at Haven Studios in Montreal, a team founded by former Assassin's Creed veteran Jade Raymond. She left the studio back in 2023, and Fairgame$ was delayed to 2026 at the time. Now the game is scrapped entirely.

According to the report, Haven "reworked" the Fairgame$ concept several times in the past three years. The studio was reportedly planning to re-reveal it with a new game. Going forward, Haven staff will support other PlayStation projects, the report said.

You can watch the original CGI reveal trailer for Fairgame$ below.

Fairgame$ was officially canceled following a playtest that didn't show strong results.

“While the test demonstrated strong operational excellence, live ops readiness and community engagement, player feedback and retention results were mixed and fell short of the goals we had set,” PlayStation executives Sean Decker and John Doyle said in a memo seen by Bloomberg. "Combined with challenging market conditions in the PVP shooter genre, we have made the difficult decision to cease development on the game.”

Creative director Mathieu Leduc said in a blog post that Haven was founded with the goal of making games that its staffers wanted to play, and that’s why the team chose a competitive multiplayer game.

“Fairgame$ came from a desire to create a new type of PvP game with emergent sandbox gameplay. We want to deliver a fresh multiplayer experience that rewards creativity and mastery and delivers surprising stories each and every time you play,” Leduc said.

“In a nutshell, this is a thrilling competitive heist game where you join an underground movement to rob the ultra-rich and rebalance the scales,” Leduc said.

As you can see in the announcement trailer, Fairgame$ has players going after billionaires who have “too much money and too much power.” In the trailer, we see a squad of players infiltrating some kind of compound, working together to take down security guards with the apparent aim of sticking it to the man.

“Fairgame$ will give you an opportunity to break the rules as a modern-day Robin Hood, a thrill seeker, or just someone who wants to collect cool loot,” Leduc said. “Trespass inside forbidden locations around the world, fill your pockets like a kid in a candy store and unravel the nefarious plans of untouchable billionaires.”

Back when Fairgame$ was announced in 2023, Sony was in the midst of a huge push and investment into the live-service market. At one point in time, Sony wanted to release 12 live-service games over the coming years (alongside its commitment to single-player games). However, in May 2023, Sony announced that it was halving its planned live-service game output, with management stressing it wanted to focus on quality over quantity. After this announcement, Naughty Dog’s The Last of Us multiplayer game was canceled in December 2023.

At the beginning of 2024, though, Sony found its biggest success to date in the live-service market with Helldivers 2–the game went on to smash sales records and become the No. 3 overall best-selling game of 2024 in the US.

In July 2024, Sony’s Destiny developer Bungie announced mass layoffs and major structural changes. A month later, Sony launched the multiplayer game Concord. It had such a dismal performance out of the gate that Sony quickly took the game offline and refunded all players. Its developer, Firewalk, was later closed.

At the end of 2024, Sony confirmed that it canceled multiple projects, including a live-service God of War and another live-service title from Bend.

It was reported in 2023 that PlayStation boss Jim Ryan, who left Sony in 2024, had a mandate that Sony’s teams should make more games-as-a-service titles. A number of PlayStation developers were reportedly upset with this, and the blame was said to have fallen not on Ryan but Connie Booth, one of the most important and veteran PlayStation developers, leading to her eventual departure.

Another former PlayStation boss, Shuhei Yoshida, said the chance of finding success in the competitive live-service market was “small,” but his replacement, Hermen Hulst, was given the resources to fund both single-player games and live-service titles at the same time. However, had Yoshida stayed in that role, he said he would have “tried to resist” the push into the live-service market. He joked, “That’s one of the reasons they removed me.”

Apple’s first foldable has issues, but here’s why I love it anyway

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

I’ve been pretty vocal about what I don’t like about the iPhone Duo so far, from the lack of a telephoto zoom and missing Face ID to the unoptimized apps and hefty weight. (Why can’t this thing be as light as the Galaxy Fold 8?)

But now that I’ve been living with and testing the iPhone Duo for about a month, there’s some things that I really like about this device that I think puts it at the top of our best foldable phone list. Here are 7 reasons why I think it’s worth the $2,000 price tag.

To say that I’m a Slack power user would be an understatement. As editor in chief of Tom’s Guide, I’m constantly jumping between multiple threads, weighing in on everything from photos and production, to collaborating with other departments. And it’s really nice to be able to quickly scroll through rooms and contacts, while still seeing message content on the right.

The iPhone Duo is even smart enough to adapt the layout as you fold the device. The Galaxy Z Fold 8 app isn’t even two columns.

Slack looks pretty slick on the front screen, too, even though the menu items take up a lot of real estate on the right side. You can quickly respond with the wide keyboard without a problem.

Yup, it’s overdue, but I really appreciate being able to run two apps side by side on the iPhone Duo. For example, I can look up what to order in DoorDash while having a chat with the family in Messages.

I also like being able to easily drag and drop images from the Photos app into Google Drive without having to start all over again each time by looking up the folder name. It’s a huge time saver. To be fair, the Galaxy Fold 8 can do three apps at once, plus floating windows on top. But I’m fine with two apps for now.

Sign up to the Tom's iGuide weekly newsletter with coverage on everything from product launches to software updates, this is your go-to source for the latest updates on all the best Apple content.

You might not be able to run four apps at once, but the Multiview feature in YouTube TV on the iPhone Duo lets you watch four of your favorite shows at the same time in a grid — just like Android foldables. You can tune into the audio on any of the four windows just by taping your finger on the live video thumbnail. And you tap again to watch the show in full-screen mode. It’s one of those things you just can’t do on a regular iPhone.

For me, I like being able to toggle between multiple NFL or NCAA football games on the weekend or ESPN’s First Take and CNN during the week.

iPhone Duo: up to $1,200 off w/ trade-in + unlimited @ T-MobileT-Mobile is knocking up to $1,200 off the iPhone Duo when you switch and bring your number or when you trade-in an eligible phone and sign up a qualifying plan. The iPhone Duo features a 7.6-inch Super Retina XDR display (1,878 x 2,670) and a 5.4-inch outer display. It houses Apple's A20 Pro chipset, 12GB of RAM and 256GB of storage. Rear cameras include a 48MP main and 48MP ultrawide. In our iPhone Duo review, we said it was worth the wait with a stellar design and smart software.

Part of the reason why I don’t make many FaceTime calls is that I don’t really feel like holding up my phone the whole time. That complaint goes away with the iPhone Duo, which lets you fold the phone in half and prop it up like a laptop. When you’re in this view, you can make FaceTime calls hands free, which is nice because I like to talk with my hands anyway.

The 4MP FaceTime camera isn’t the sharpest, but it gets the job done.

If there’s one app that I would show people if I had 30 seconds to explain why the iPhone Duo is cool, it would be Netflix. The app has been developed from the ground up for this foldable, and it shows.

For example, on the cover display you can skim through mobile-friendly shorts that fill the screen, like Instagram or TikTok. As you’d expect, shows and movies look great on the large 7.6-inch display, as I discovered when watching “The Diplomat” on a long flight. But if you want to snack while you’re watching, you can put the Duo in tabletop mode so your video is up top and controls down below. Or, if you prefer, you can watch in tent mode.

Standby is one of my favorite iPhone features from the past few years, because you can turn your device into an alarm clock when you’re ready to go to bed. But the iPhone Duo takes that to the next level. You get a clock when you put the Duo in tent mode, and when it’s time to get up a soft glow emanates from the inside of the foldable to help wake you up.

Plus, there’s another Standby mode. When you put the Duo in portrait mode and fold it half-way standing up on a table or desk, you’ll see a clock and calendar on the left and some of your favorite photos on the right. It’s like a digital photo frame. Plus, you can still easily access Spotify in this mode via the Dynamic Island.

Because the iPhone Duo weighs down my front pocket when walking around, I’ve mostly defaulted to carrying it in my back pocket. And lots of times I’ve sat on this foldable phone — forgetting to take it out first, whether I’m sitting at my desk at the office or just plopping down to watch TV at night.

At least so far, the iPhone Duo has survived my daily use without a scratch or crack. The titanium frame feels super durable to me, and even after a few weeks the crease is not prominent at all when using this device.

#3611. Kate Middleton Dresses Down for Appearance at Mental Health-Focused Charity

During a surprise engagement in West London, Kate Middleton reminded fans that she is the queen of country-set dressing. Prince William's wife joined the team at Dose of Nature, a charity that “prescribes” time spent outdoors to help improve mental health, telling staff members and volunteers that connecting with nature is a “healing” experience for her.

The future queen dressed down for the occasion, wrapping up warm in what looked to be a Barbour jacket and a pair of jeans. She left her hair to flow in waves and accessorized with her trademark “big blue” sapphire engagement ring.

At Pensford Field, where Dose of Nature has a site near Kew, the Princess of Wales met the charity's founder, Dr. Alison Greenwood, and clinical lead, Dr. Georgina Gould, as well as volunteer nature guide Tom, who told Catherine that support from Dose of Nature had made him more confident and resilient.

“Our journey has been very very different, but it’s so wonderful to hear how your nature connection and how it’s been so healing for you, and I felt the same,” Catherine said to him.

“The fact that you’re able to provide that to so many other people in this community; that sense of purpose and meaning, and belonging, through that experience, I think is something that has got the longevity and the sustainability of feeling like, almost without knowing what’s to come, without having the control in your life of knowing what the future might hold, the fact that you feel that you can cope with things, because you feel that interconnection, I think that makes it holistic in a very true essence,” she added.

The Princess of Wales visits Dose of Nature.

Kate Middleton has long been a champion of the importance of nature for mental and physical well-being. In a recent essay, she wrote: “By spending time in nature or being creative, we can nurture the very skills and emotions that cannot be digitised: awareness, empathy, humility, and above all, love.”

The future queen has been working with the Royal Foundation Centre for Early Childhood on a project to “support the healthy development of babies and young children,” as she explained in a recent video, delivered from Cornwall while dressed in ME+EM.

“In this tech-driven, digital age, spending time outdoors has never been more important,” the Princess said.

“This project is about how nature, creativity, and relationships can best support the healthy development of babies and young children,” she continued. “My hope is that through this practical, nature-based research, we can build supportive environments that help make nature more accessible, benefiting babies, young children, and their families across the UK.”

The Princess of Wales has spent many years dedicated to early childhood research, working hard advising the Foundation, even during her cancer treatment. This May, she visited the University of East London’s Institute for the Science of Early Years and Youth to see how the University’s researchers use state-of-the-art wearables and brain recording techniques to study how the diverse early living environments and relationships experienced by babies influence early stress—both in the child themselves and their parents and caregivers.

#3610. Law and Order: SVU's Dean Winters, 62, Confirms Romance With Glori Dei, 28

Law and Order: SVU alum Dean Winters confirmed his romance with model and fellow actor Glori Dei Filippone, who is nearly 34 years his junior.

The couple attended a special screening of Ebenezer in New York earlier this month. Filippone, 28, who is nonbinary, took to Instagram on Sunday, November 8, to share more photos of them and Winters, 62, writing, “Til the wheels fall off.”

In response, one commenter wrote “hard launch” on the joint post, to which Winters replied, “Nothing soft here.” Another social media user wrote, “U guys r gorgeous together,” and Winters responded, “Thank you brother, can’t wait for you to meet her!!”

Winters is best known for his role as Ryan in Oz, in addition to appearances on Millennium, Rescue Me, 30 Rock, Sex and the City and Brooklyn Nine-Nine. He has also become synonymous with the character Mayhem from a series of Allstate Insurance commercials.

Many TV fans, however, are familiar with Winters for his work on Law & Order: Special Victims Unit. He was a series regular in season 1 when Detective Brian Cassidy was part of the team before ultimately asking to be moved to Narcotics. Off screen, Winter stepped away because of a contractual obligation to HBO’s Oz.

“I was on the show for the first season, but then I had to leave because I had a contract with HBO, and there was a bit of a dispute,” Winters revealed to The A.V. Club in 2015.

Winters returned in season 13 — more than 10 years after his last appearance on SVU. He became a recurring character in the 14th and 15th seasons as Brian and Olivia (Mariska Hargitay) started dating.

“But how it happened was that I was in my apartment, and there was a film crew setting up outside my apartment,” the actor recalled to the outlet. “It was 5 a.m., and I was trying to go to bed, but everyone’s making a lot of noise, so I lean out my window, and I yell, ‘Would you guys shut the f*** up?’ And Richard Belzer yells back up. I had no idea it was SVU!”

He continued: “So I went outside and saw everyone, and then I went over to Mariska’s trailer to say hi, and she was, like, ‘How come you’ve never come back on the show?’ And I said, ‘No one’s ever asked me!’ And the following week I was back on the show!”

Brian and Olivia ultimately parted ways, and Winters has not been back on the show outside of a brief return in 2025.
