#3543. Stephen Miller Into the Breach: How Susie Wiles’s Failures Portend Miller’s Future

There’s a time-honored tradition for new White House chiefs of staff: The outgoing chief invites former holders of the office, Republicans and Democrats, to a get-together (usually in the West Wing), where the newcomer is offered advice. But Donald Trump’s new chief, Stephen Miller—appointed in a jaw-dropping Truth Social post on Friday—won’t be getting a party. First, because the tradition applies only to a president’s first chief. Second, because no Democratic chief would likely want to be caught dead with Miller, a longtime basher of the opposition party. Shortly after hearing that Trump had picked the hard-right firebrand as his new chief, James Carville sent me a text that summed up the prevailing attitude: “This is like Caligula’s appointment of his horse as consul.”

It was different when Susie Wiles came to town. On the evening of November 19, 2024, she was the guest of honor at a dinner party thrown by Jeffrey Zients, Joe Biden’s outgoing White House chief of staff. They were joined by eight of Zients’s predecessors. It was an occasion for bipartisan bonhomie, a tradition started in 2008 by George W. Bush’s chief Joshua Bolten. In a spirit of goodwill and generosity, Bolten had thrown a gathering in his West Wing office for Barack Obama’s incoming chief, Rahm Emanuel. The informal meetup was intended as a way to convey the chiefs’ collective wisdom and experience—and to offer, in miniature, a nuts-and-bolts version of the transition of executive power that is a hallmark of American democracy.

Now evicted from her West Wing corner office, with the president’s agenda in tatters, Wiles has learned that fealty to Trump almost always ends badly.

On the night of the dinner for Wiles, however, a cloud hung over the occasion. Virtually no one at the table thought she could succeed as Donald Trump’s chief of staff.

For almost two years, Wiles was the second most powerful person in the West Wing. Had Trump been interested in governing, she might have helped him solidify a GOP majority in Congress for years to come. But she was unwilling, or unable, to save Trump from himself. On Wiles’s watch, he squandered his second term with a reign of revenge, retribution, and recklessness. Now evicted from her West Wing corner office, with the president’s agenda in tatters, Wiles has learned that fealty to Trump almost always ends badly.

And if past experience is any guide, Wiles’s replacement, Stephen Miller, may well crash and burn in even more spectacular fashion.

There was no one the president relied on or trusted more than Wiles. From their first meeting in 2015 at Trump Tower to her impressive stint as his winning 2024 presidential campaign co-manager, the “ice maiden” had Trump’s back. And he had hers—until last Tuesday’s epic Democratic blowout. Wiles would resign two days later. Indeed, the Republicans’ midterm apocalypse was an extinction event that not even Wiles could have survived.

Ironically, Trump’s savvy political strategist was the architect of what turned out to be a big blue bloodbath. “We’re going to win the midterms,” Wiles told me boldly when I interviewed her for Vanity Fair just a year ago. Even then, three months before Trump initiated a war on Iran, that was a ridiculously rosy prediction. The president’s approval rating was in the gutter. He’d failed to address, much less solve, voters’ primary concerns: affordability, inflation, health care, and housing—and had still not released the remaining Epstein files. How could a battle-hardened political pro like Wiles be so starry-eyed? The answer, I believe, is that in the fog of MAGA-land, she’d lost touch with the real world.

In almost every presidency, the West Wing is a bubble where like-minded acolytes engage in groupthink. But in Trump’s West Wing this phenomenon is exponentially magnified. It’s a parallel universe, one in which the 2020 election was stolen, violent insurrectionists are “patriots,” and the prosecution of political enemies—with scant evidence—is a presidential perk. (“Who would blame him?” Wiles said to me of Trump’s campaign to settle scores.) That, to my mind, is why Wiles seemed so stunned by the firestorm that erupted when her words appeared in my 10,000-word Vanity Fair series last December. She had no idea they would land like bombs on planet Earth.

Wiles invested Trump with almost otherworldly powers. He would lead the GOP to victory in the 2026 midterms, she believed, because of his preternatural ability to rally his base. That’s why, on the eve of the midterms, Wiles was all-in on sending Trump almost everywhere all at once, admonishing people to “vote like I’m on the ballot.” The trouble was voters saw all too clearly what she apparently couldn’t see: Trump was deeply unpopular; on his watch, the country was coming apart.

A year ago, when Wiles made her electoral prediction, I challenged her. “I admire your confidence about the midterms,” I said, “but the stakes are huge, right? And history is not encouraging. Incumbents do stuff and there’s a reaction. And usually, as Obama said, you get shellacked.”

Wiles seemed to shrug off that possibility. “Can you ever imagine Donald Trump saying that?” she said. “No, no.”

Wiles was right. Trump could never say such a thing—because he could never accept the fact that his electoral magic had waned. Neither, it seemed, could Wiles. But as his chief of staff and top political strategist, she was paid to know better.

Even before the election debacle, Trump had reportedly started privately inquiring about her on phone calls, although he lashed out at accounts of such purported conversations. Then, once the carnage sunk in, the die was cast. Wiles offered her resignation. And Trump accepted it.

At the start of her West Wing tenure, I believed Wiles stood a chance of succeeding. If Trump would listen to anyone, I thought, it was the loyal, organized, no-nonsense Wiles. Yet during 10 conversations with her over 10 months, I watched as she abdicated the most important duty of the White House chief: telling the president hard truths. Wiles told me she’d read my book, The Gatekeepers: How the White House Chiefs of Staff Define Every Presidency, and she understood the importance of heeding Reagan chief James Baker’s advice. “You do not serve your president well if you are just a yes man,” he said. In a phone call, she told me, Baker “reminded me that my job wasn’t to be a fangirl.” I asked Wiles, “Have you had any gut check moments where you had to tell the president something he didn’t want to hear?” She paused. “I probably have one a day,” she said. “But they’re over little things, not big.”

Wiles should have known that the midterms would spell disaster. She carried around a list of her priorities, on an index card. Number five: “Don’t forget about organized labor. Don’t forget about young Black men and women and Hispanics…because that’s the future of the country and the backbone of his support. And if we don’t convert those people to being enthusiastic Republicans, then if the Democrats were even just a little bit better, they might win an election.”

Miller is a zealot, a hard-boiled ideologue—an advocate of Trump’s notorious first-term Muslim ban, the brutal paramilitary tactics of ICE, the deployment of the National Guard to Democrat-run cities, and the lethal air strikes on boats in the Caribbean.

They might—and they did. And now Wiles is out, taking up shop, so Trump himself has said, within his political operation. Last November she hinted that she knew this day might come: “You go to bed at night, you say your prayers, you take stock of what the day was and what your day is tomorrow, and you get up and do it again…. So as long as that’s the case and the president’s pleased…” Wiles paused. “He could fire you tomorrow.”

She’s sensitive about her legacy as the first female White House chief. “I’m not an enabler,” she insisted. “I’m also, like, not a bitch. I try to be thoughtful about what I engage in, and what I disagree [with the president] about. I guess time will tell whether I’ve been effective.”

What about Wiles’s successor, Stephen Miller?

Miller is the antithesis of Ronald Reagan’s chief James Baker, a cool pragmatist who could push back on the president’s half-baked ideas. Miller, by contrast, is a zealot, a hard-boiled ideologue—an advocate of Trump’s notorious first-term Muslim ban, the brutal paramilitary tactics of ICE, the deployment of the National Guard to Democrat-run cities, and the lethal air strikes on boats in the Caribbean. He believes in a Hobbesian world, he has stated, “that is governed by strength, that is governed by force, that is governed by power.” Now he’ll be the last person in the room when Trump makes life-and-death decisions about law and order and war and peace.

The man who decreed that the president’s powers “are very substantial and will not be questioned” is now the official charged with questioning the president’s decisions. It’s hard to imagine Miller doing that without a personality transplant. He’s already alienated the House minority leader, and soon to be Speaker, Hakeem Jeffries, who has called Miller “a dangerous xenophobe and reckless extremist who has American blood on his hands,” insisting, “I’ve got zero interest in working with that kind of individual.”

At the White House last November, after a Vanity Fair photo session, I spoke with Miller at length about the midterms, still a year away; about his portfolio in the Trump administration; and about the role of the White House chief of staff. Perched on a chair in the Roosevelt Room, he eyed me warily. He seemed impatient to get back to work. “I understand that your need for me is quite limited, right?” he said.

I asked Miller about his interactions with the president—specifically an Oval Office meeting in which he and Trump reportedly talked about blowing up boats in the Caribbean. “I would never talk about…whether a meeting occurred or didn’t occur,” he said, “or whether it was in a meeting that did occur, or was not in that meeting if it occurred, which I would never say either way.”

Miller was more forthcoming about Wiles’s prediction—that Trump and the GOP would triumph at the polls in 2026. “What about you?” I asked him. “I am confident that we’ll win the midterms,” he replied. History might be against them, he said, “but we have every expectation that we’re going to defy that history.” “Why?” I asked. Miller replied, “Because of the president’s unprecedentedly successful first nine months in office.”

What followed was a black-is-white, up-is-down litany of Trump’s accomplishments, a revisionist history that might have made Karoline Leavitt, another world-class propagandist, blush. “In no particular order,” Miller said, “the taming and defeating of inflation. As you know, we inherited record double-digit inflation and the president made his first priority to bring down the cost of living…cutting the price of energy by high double digits. For many Americans, gas prices have been cut in half since we took over.” None of this, of course, has proved true—but Miller was just warming up.

“And the passage of the largest package of tax cuts and reforms in American history in the form of the One Big Beautiful Bill. Fully securing the Southern border, the most secure border in history, zero illegal crossings, four months in a row. And also the largest number of deportations in American history…. The president has…achieved more in foreign policy than any president in our lifetimes, ending eight wars in eight months—which includes, but is not limited to, securing the historic peace deal between Israel and Gaza, Thailand and Cambodia, Congo and Rwanda, Azerbaijan and Armenia, Israel and Iran, and so on…”

Miller still wasn’t done. The president, he said, “has executed on every promise he’s made to the American people and that includes also taking back our culture and fighting against whether you call it radical leftism or woke or Marxism—a lot of people just call it plain crazy—but taking back our culture and restoring sanity to American life.

“It is my extraordinary privilege and blessing,” Miller added, “to be able to work for the president of the United States, to implement an agenda that I believe in wholly and completely and with every fiber of my being.”

I was there, of course, because I was writing a story on Susie Wiles and her West Wing team. I asked him, point-blank: “Would you agree, though, that it’s also the chief of staff’s job to tell the president what he doesn’t want to hear?”

“No, I wouldn’t say that,” Miller replied, finding fault with my framing of the question and insisting that this president wants to hear everything. “The chief of staff would never have to encounter the scenario you’re describing.” Miller said. “President Trump craves, he loves the every-minute detail of management, having every piece of information, having every side of everything, having inputs into the Oval Office from every square, every quarter, every person.”

As for the president’s staff, Miller said, their job is “implementing the president’s vision, the president’s directions, the president’s agenda, the president’s plans for the future…. We’re just here on his behalf to see that that is done.”

As the great political columnist Molly Ivins once wrote, “It probably sounded better in the original German.”

Chris Whipple is a contributing writer at Vanity Fair and a Fall 2026 Resident Fellow at Harvard’s Kennedy School Institute of Politics. You can follow him on Substack.

#3542. If You Loved 'Below,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Foggy, cold, and hardscrabble, the community of Snook’s Arm, Newfoundland, is the perfect spot for ocean-borne horror in Netflix's Below. This sense of place sets the series apart, though the characters who inhabit it are equally fascinating. Led by Josh Hartnett’s grounded performance as Calvin, the show has atmosphere for days, and a creepy and compelling story that effortlessly balances chills and deep emotional beats.

If you ate this show up like a voracious sea creature and you’re craving more slow-burn, deeply human horror (and you’ve already explored all the similar streaming series out there), it’s time to move on to feature-length terror, and there's one classic movie that fits the bill.

When it comes to kindred sea monster stories, Jaws is the obvious choice. Seaside setting? Check—a pre-glam Martha’s Vineyard stands in for Amity Island, with beautiful beaches and crashing waves to spare. A tight community under threat? Check—Amity Island feels like a very real place, and its citizens have concerns and grudges as legitimate as Calvin’s in Below. Shocks and frights? This is Jaws, a film that transformed the entire business of blockbuster movies, renowned to this day for its masterful depiction of a relentless natural force threatening an entire town.

The basic story also echoes Below's: When a young woman is killed by a shark during a night swim, Amity Island Police Chief Martin Brody (Roy Scheider) tries to close the beaches to protect the public, but Mayor Vaughn (Murray Hamilton) refuses, as Amity Island depends on the tourist trade for its survival. After a young boy is killed, Brody teams up with shark hunter Quint (Robert Shaw) and oceanographer Hooper (Richard Dreyfuss) to hunt the beast, and the three soon find themselves in over their heads as they discover how big and relentless the shark really is. Both stories share themes of economic necessity trumping safety in a changing world and concepts of a small group of people fighting a terrifying natural threat.

Like almost every horror film or series since 1975, Below owes a debt to Jaws in terms of storytelling and technique. From the isolated, ocean-centric setting (and monster) to the way Below shows you only flashes of its central terror, if you enjoyed the series, you will absolutely love the classic that influenced it. Stream Jaws on Netflix, or rent it on Prime Video.

Already seen Jaws, or rewatched it, and still in need of more terrifying movies in the same vein as Below? Here are a few more movies that you’ll love.

The Bay takes a different approach to its scares than Below—it’s a found-footage horror film. But it shares the remote, water-centric setting, the focus on a small community, and a story that pulls from the terror of a fundamental element—water—being polluted and corrupted. In the coastal community of Claridge, Maryland, citizens fall severely ill and begin dying in large numbers, sparking chaos. As investigators race to discover the source of the affliction, the carnage gets seriously gnarly. Just like in Below, the ultimate threat stems from the way people recklessly abuse the world we depend on for survival, and the local residents are center stage in the fight. Stream The Bay on Tubi or rent it on Prime Video.

One aspect of Below that resonates strongly with viewers is the human element; the Penney family’s internal tensions feel earned and real, and the way the larger community struggles with several existential crises is messy in a gloriously human way. The Host is also about a family struggling against a horrific, waterborne monster—when a mutant creature attacks a crowd near the Han River, Park Gang-du loses his grip on his young daughter, and she’s snatched up by the monster. But when Gang-du receives a phone call from his daughter telling him she’s still alive but trapped with the creature in the sewers, his family escapes quarantine, gears up, and goes after her, no matter the odds (or the corrupt government agencies standing in the way). Stream The Host on Kanopy or rent it on Prime Video.

Based on H.P. Lovecraft’s The Shadow Over Innsmouth, Dagon begins with four friends on a boat off the coast of Spain. When a storm wrecks the boat and injures one of them, a couple—Paul and Barbara—travel on foot to a nearby village to seek help. What they find instead is a terrifying place paying the price for worshiping a demon named Dagon in exchange for wealth and safety—but at a price that slowly rose, eventually transforming the villagers into something inhuman. Just like Below, the movie explores the choices communities make to survive, and the personal costs that aren’t always clearly understood. Stream Dagon on The Roku Channel or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

If you loved Below’s foggy, liminal feel and the constant dread of what might be lurking in the mist or under the waves, unseen until it’s too late, John Carpenter’s classic is a must-watch. As the small coastal town of Antonio Bay approaches the centennial of its founding, a strange fog rolls in from the sea and envelopes the town. As the body count rises, the true story of the town’s founding and subsequent prosperity is revealed—and the long-deferred price for the crimes of the town’s ancestors is in the fog, determined to find some element of justice. Stream The Fog on Kanopy or Plex, or rent it on Prime Video.

If remote communities like Snook’s Arm are inherently creepy to you, check out Offseason. When Marie (Jocelin Donahue) learns that her mother has passed away and has been buried in Lone Palm, the isolated beach town where she grew up, she’s outraged—her mother was very clear that she didn’t want to be buried there. Marie travels to Lone Palm as tourist season ends, just a day before the bridge to the mainland closes for the year, which gives the town a liminal, nightmarish aspect familiar to anyone who’s lived in a tourist town during the offseason. As a storm moves in, Marie and her boyfriend find the townsfolk behaving quite strangely—and soon, it all whips up into a maelstrom of terror that fans of Below will appreciate. Stream Offseason on Hoopla or rent it on Prime Video.

#3541. I Tested Strava's New Integration With Gemini, and I Have Thoughts

Once connected, you can ask questions like:

"Am I getting faster at the same heart rate?"

"Can you give me a detailed analysis of how I performed in my last race?"

"How is my strength training impacting my running?"

Some important context here: Strava's AI "insights" have sort of sucked, and annoyed me, in the past. Athlete Intelligence (conveniently abbreviated as AI) is the Strava feature that writes text responses to your workouts. Strava calls these "insights," but as far as I can tell they mostly regurgitate the information from the workout description, sometimes with added errors. I've found AI fitness summaries largely useless, and Strava's version checks every box: It doesn't use enough context to understand what's going on, it presents generic advice as if it were personal, and it's overconfident in incomplete data. So, skeptical as I am, I gave Strava's latest Google Gemini integration a whirl. Here's what it does, how to set it up, and whether it's worth it.

The first question I asked was one of Strava’s examples, "Am I getting faster at the same heart rate?" Gemini said yes, I was seeing solid efficiency gains. Like many AI tools, it told me what I wanted to hear. I had to point out that heat and temperature are huge variables. When I steered the chat in that direction, Gemini, of course, agreed immediately ("you hit the nail on the head") and explained that my mid-September long runs happened in 75–84°F weather with higher humidity, which inflates heart rate, while October's cooler temperatures made the same effort look better. That's an important caveat the first answer left out entirely.

I then asked it to compare my past marathons, and in many ways, I had fun here. For instance, the suggested follow-ups prompted me to think of questions I hadn't put on my list, like comparing my weekly running volume and long-run frequency leading into different races in different years.

Unfortunately, the results weren't reliable at first. When I asked for a detailed analysis of every marathon-distance effort since 2019, Gemini said I had exactly one, the Marine Corps Marathon on October 25, 2026. In reality, I've logged at least eight. When I asked why it couldn't see them, it explained that its access is limited to my recent history, roughly summer 2026 onward, because of how pagination limits the number of past activities returned at once. It also offered a workaround: Give it specific dates and locations.

That workaround works, but it means you have to already know what you're looking for. And still, it wasn't consistent. In other answers, Gemini referenced my 2025 NYC Marathon and 2024 Philadelphia race, so the data's reach seems uneven. You need to be able to query older date ranges as directly and specifically as possible, and even still, double-check any numbers that matter to you.

I then asked "What am I doing right and what am I doing wrong as a runner?" After knowing the queries need to be so specific, I intentionally wanted to test a vague, simplistic question. The answer was, true to form, overly flattering—though I didn't disagree with the guidance itself. I need more speed workouts! I know this! I didn't need a chatbot to tell me, though maybe some other Strava user does. Gemini's suggestions (polarize training, add one dedicated threshold day) are sound, yes, but they’re also generic. Most recreational runners could glance at my Strava and spot the same strengths and weaknesses. Similarly, Gemini then set itself up for a slam dunk by prompting me to ask whether my easy runs were too fast. The answer: My easy days were happening at nearly my marathon pace (about 9:43/mi), and I should slow down by 45–90 seconds per mile, to roughly 10:30–11:15/mi. I completely agree. That being said, my big takeaway here remains the same: Don't confuse AI-generated advice as some newfound, personalized insight. It’s often the same conventional wisdom you already know, or could figure out with a tiny bit of research from a real, human source.

If you ask me—a human!—this is a classic case of using AI for rote tasks, but then saving critical thinking for your own human brain. Gemini didn't surface anything wildly insightful, and it skipped important considerations like the effect of heat on heart rate, until I raised them myself. But it pulled data faster than I could have by hand, and its follow-up prompts nudged me toward comparisons I might not have thought of.

For many users, the smartest approach may be to skip AI summaries and focus on raw data. After all, your training load, sleep duration, and heart rate trends are already perfectly actionable.

As with all things AI, it’s important to mind the gap between data and wisdom. So much wisdom gets lost—forfeited, even—when you blindly trust an AI coach. Make sure you aren’t offloading all the other skills you need as a runner and as a human, like your ability to listen to your body and maybe run a little slower in the heat, even when it makes your data look “worse.”

If you do use Google Gemini to analyze your Strava data:

Be specific about dates and locations when asking about older activities.

Push back. Ask about weather, terrain, and fatigue before accepting a flattering conclusion.

Treat the output as a fast data pull, not a personal coach.

60 Minutes has entered a new era amid the 2026 TV schedule, and a person who’s been overseeing much of the work behind the scenes is CBS News Editor-in-Chief Bari Weiss. In conjunction with the news magazine show’s EP, Nick Bilton, Weiss has been looking to update the program, and those efforts have been accompanied by major staff changes and backlash. Some of the criticisms have come from former staff members, including ex-EP Bill Owens, who recently shared his biggest concerns over the series he once shepherded.

Owens worked at CBS News for 37 years and, in 2019, he was named the EP of 60 Minutes after having spent 12 years overseeing its content in other roles. He ultimately resigned from his post in April 2025 amid a flurry of behind-the-scenes changes at 60. Since his departure, Owens has discussed his time with the show, and he notably shared thoughts ahead of the Season 59 premiere, which aired in September. At Semafor’s New Media & Marketing Playbook event, Owens was asked for his thoughts on his former workplace and said:

Not a lot. [Skydance owns] the company, they can do whatever they want. But the ratings are telling. There’s no doubt that linear television is in decline. But the numbers the other day were less than 6 million people. It’s like the evening news. 60 Minutes? That would have freaked me out.

Ratings for the latest season of 60 have reportedly been down compared to those of Season 58. The season premiere notched lower viewership and, despite some forward progress in subsequent weeks, more recent numbers haven’t been so strong. For instance, per data on the show’s October 25 broadcast, the episode only drew 5.6 million live viewers, which fell well below Season 58’s 9.1 million average. Despite that, when Bari Weiss addressed concerns, she stated that the show was doing “tremendously well.”

As for Owens, he’s been candid about leaving 60 Minutes, and he has attributed that move to no longer having the editorial independence he and his colleagues had long been granted. During the Semafor event, Owens also criticized the show’s interview with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and argued that better questions should’ve been asked. On a separate note, the veteran journalist also admitted that he wished his departure would’ve had a different effect on 60:

When I left, I really hoped that I was going to cause enough of a commotion that they would kind of back off. And the people, my senior team, the correspondents, they’ve tried their best. But it’s just a really difficult circumstance.

May 2026 marked the beginning of major personnel changes at 60 Minutes, as several high-profile staffers were let go, including correspondents Sharyn Alfonsi and Cecilia Vega as well as former EP Tanya Simon. Days later, fellow host Scott Pelley was fired as well after he reportedly accused Weiss of “murdering” the show. Around that time, Owens defended Pelley’s comments, saying that he “stood up the way that I did a year ago and I couldn’t be prouder of him, and I know all the people at 60 Minutes couldn’t be prouder of him.”

Bill Owens has since moved on to other ventures and, beginning in March 2027, he’ll executive-produce a YouTube-based outlet known as NewPress. It’s also been rumored that Owens will spill tea about his time at 60 Minutes through a tell-all memoir, but that’s yet to materialize. At the very least, though, Owens still seems somewhat interested about what the future holds for 60.

He graduated from the University of Maryland, where he received a degree in Broadcast Journalism. After shifting into multi-platform journalism, he started working as a freelance writer and editor before joining CB. Covers superheroes, sci-fi, comedy, and almost anything else in film and TV. He eats more pizza than the Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles.

#3538. Why Those Flashy Halloween Contacts Are a Bad Idea

Contacts with cat pupils or neon colors can be fun, but are you sure you want to put a piece of plastic from a costume store into your eye? Experts, like those at the American Academy of Ophthalmology, warn against it. These non-prescription contacts are technically illegal in the U.S. (even though plenty of companies sell them anyway). The CDC warns that the risks include "eye sores and vision loss."

Cheap Halloween contacts tend to be one-size-fits-all, but the AAO points out that contacts should never be one-size-fits-all. A contact that is too large or too small for your eye can cause corneal abrasions, corneal ulcers, and can result in infections like keratitis. Infections can, in severe cases, lead to blindness. A 2017 report from the FDA found bacterial contamination in 27% of costume contacts.

If you do wear contacts (Halloween or otherwise), the AAO recommends keeping an eye out for symptoms like redness, swelling, pain, or excessive discharge. Seek care as soon as you suspect an infection. Your eyes are more sensitive to infections than other parts of the body, so be cautious.

Legally, contacts require a prescription, so if those colored contacts you're eyeing can be bought without showing a doctor’s prescription, they’re not legit. The real thing can be expensive, though: I found prices of $40 and up from lens.com, Discount Contacts, and Wicked Eyez.

These websites all let you order online, but you’ll have to provide your prescription information before you can check out. Fortunately, the Federal Trade Commission has ruled that providers must give you your contact prescription after a fitting so that you can take the prescription elsewhere. And they cannot charge you extra for this.

Once you’ve got the lenses, you have to know how to take care of them. If you wear contacts every day, you already know the drill. But if you’re just picking up a pair to use with a costume, here are the basics:

Wash your hands before handling the lenses.

Store them in contact lens solution, and keep the lenses and their case clean.

And for Pete’s sake, don’t share them with your friends!

Just remember, the bloodshot look stops being cool after you take your zombie costume off.

#3537. The Role of the “Queen Mother” in Monarchies Around the World: Queen Sofía, Sonia of Norway, and Beatrix of the Netherlands

Queen Sofía celebrated her 88th birthday on November 2 and remains a pillar of the Spanish royal family, with a demanding schedule that includes at least one official engagement per week. Queen Sofía has never set aside her institutional role, unlike some other European “queen mothers” (this official title is used only in the United Kingdom but is commonly used to refer to the mothers of kings), who, to a greater or lesser extent, continue to work for the monarchy in their respective countries.

This week, Queen Sofía will be in San Fernando, Cádiz, where she will serve as patroness of the ceremony to present the National Ensign to the Marine Corps, a special unit within the Navy and the world’s oldest marine corps, created in 1537 by Emperor Charles I. Far from retiring from public life, the Queen Emerita continues to play an important role within the Crown; she retains her office at Zarzuela and receives an official stipend.

She also remains closely involved in the day-to-day activities of the Queen Sofía Foundation and regularly visits the provincial offices of the Spanish Federation of Food Banks to learn about its charitable work, among other projects. Always discreet, Felipe VI’s mother has weathered the controversies surrounding Juan Carlos and maintained a professional image dedicated to serving the Spanish people—one that her family circumstances have not tarnished.

Queen Sonja, a great source of support today for her son, King Haakon.

Following the death of her husband, King Harald, in late August, and with the newly crowned Queen Mette-Marit on medical leave, Queen Sonja of Norway has become a pillar of support for her son, Haakon VIII. Sonia of Norway is 89 years old and in recent months has had minor health scares that led to her being hospitalized for a few days in the hospital. But despite everything, she continues her duties as a member of the Norwegian royal family. Just a few days ago, Queen Sonja traveled to Málaga to attend the opening of an exhibition on Picasso and Munch at the Picasso Museum in the Andalusian city, and was all smiles during a visit to a Norwegian school in Benalmádena.

On November 3, Queen Sonja accompanied her son Haakon to an official dinner to welcome the provincial governors at the Royal Palace—an important event at which the king will have his mother’s support in the absence of his wife and his daughter, Crown Princess Ingrid Alexandra, who is currently focused on her university studies in Oslo. Two days later, Queen Sonja will visit the Furniture Maker School in Askim, attend the opening of a furniture exhibition at the Center for Democracy at Fort Høytorp, and meet with members of the Indre Østfold Women’s Group and young people at the Re:læx youth center in Askim.

After more than three decades as queen, Sonia of Norway has stayed by her son’s side, at a time when he needs her support more than ever. Since her accession to the throne, Queen Sonia—whom Haakon stripped of the title “Her Majesty,” now simply Queen Sonia—has become a cornerstone of institutional and family support for the new monarch.

Beatrix of the Netherlands served as queen for 33 years.

At 88 years old, Beatrix of the Netherlands does not have a schedule as busy as those of Queen Sofía or Queen Sonja of Norway, but she has continued to attend institutional events and fulfill some official engagements since her abdication in 2013. King Willem-Alexander’s mother actively participates in award ceremonies linked to the Crown, such as the Appeltjes van Oranje awards presented by the Oranje Fonds foundation—awards whose bronze statuettes she designed herself and which she attends each year alongside King Willem-Alexander and Queen Máxima.

In addition, Princess Beatrix continues to make official trips to the Dutch Caribbean territories (such as her recent visits to Bonaire, St. Eustatius, and Saba) to preside over events dedicated to nature conservation, sustainable development, and education. She also continues to attend certain cultural and charitable events in her home country, such as the Dutch Ballet Gala hosted by the Dansersfonds Foundation, which she attended in mid-October.

Beatrix of the Netherlands, who now resides at Drakenstein Castle, was Queen of the Netherlands for 33 years, from 1980 to 2013. Following the coronation of her son Willem, she regained the title of princess, and today her official title is Her Royal Highness Princess Beatrix of the Netherlands, Princess of Orange-Nassau, and Princess of Lippe-Biesterfeld. Beatrix of the Netherlands remains deeply loved and respected by the people, and within the Orange-Nassau royal family, she continues to support and guide her son, King Willem-Alexander.

Princess Beatrix is a great role model for her granddaughter, Princess Amalia.

Queen Sofía, Queen Sonja of Norway, and Beatrix of the Netherlands all embody the key institutional values essential to preserving the monarchy in their respective countries. Loyal to the crown in one capacity or another and having dedicated their lives to public service for decades, all three are great examples of institutional loyalty for their granddaughters— Princess Leonor, Princess Ingrid Alexandra, and Princess Amalia—who will one day become queens.

#3536. One of the Best QLED TVs of 2026 Is Over $1,300 Off Right Now

TCL has been pushing the boundaries of QLED TVs, making some of the best in the market at very competitive prices. This year, the company released its QM8L model, introducing a new design and impressive features and specs to a series that isn't even their flagship. Right now, the 65-inch QM8L is $1,197.99 (originally $2,499.99), $100 cheaper than it was just earlier this month, reaching its lowest price since it launched in April, according to price-tracking tools. Larger sizes are also seeing substantial discounts.

One of the first things you'll notice about the QM8L is the “Zero Border” bezel design, which gives it a modern, minimalistic look. When you turn it on, you'll likely note how bright this TV gets, which is a huge advantage QLEDs have over OLEDs. TCL claims it reaches 6,000 nits—seeing as the brightest OLED TV on the market only reaches 700 nits, no OLED can come close to this unit's brightness. Another important spec to note here is the local dimming zones: TCL claims this TV has up to 4,000, which means it gets top-tier backlight control, limited light blooming (thanks in part to TCL's "Halo Control"), and incredible contrast levels that some might not be able to distinguish from an OLED.

As many of us won't manually calibrate our TVs, the picture modes you can switch to in the settings will be most people's go-to. This TV's "Filmmaker mode" provides accurate color and picture, and if you're a gamer, you can use the native 144Hz high-refresh rate. If you don't already have a surround sound system at home and want to keep a minimalist setup, the QM8L comes with Dolby Atmos-ready Bang & Olufsen speakers, which offer above-average audio output compared to most TVs. You can read more about these features in CNET's 8.8/10 review. If 65 inches isn't quite right for your home theater setup, take a look at the QM8L's other sizes, which are also discounted right now.

"Merry Memories"Stars: Lindura, Brendan MorganLogline: Michaela (Lindura) is a rigid accountant who steps in to help her brother care for his young son Danny (Omi Fitzpatrick-Gonzales) while Danny’s military mom is deployed over Christmas. When Danny is assigned to create a holiday scrapbook for his mom, Michaela reluctantly accepts help from his free-spirited substitute teacher, Bryan (Morgan), whose creativity clashes with her need for preciseness and control. As they set out to capture festive moments for the scrapbook unexpected mishaps turn into meaningful traditions – and sparks begin to fly. Through Danny’s project, Michaela learns to embrace imperfection and open her heart, while Bryan rethinks his future as a traveling substitute teacher.

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

"Holiday Unplugged"Stars: Nikki DeLoach, Juan Pablo Di PaceLogline: Sally (DeLoach), an art teacher, has spent the last 10 years honoring the memory of her late husband Jake while raising their children, Keegan (Brandon Ironside) and Boo (Remy Marthaller). Feeling like she’s finally ready for love, she joins a dating app and is matched with Damon (Di Pace), her former colleague who taught her kids’ kindergarten class. Jake had co-founded a web platform that preserved family home videos. When a server migration wipes out Sally’s treasured videos of him – and her phone containing backup copies accidentally shatters – the only hope is finding the original tapes. She doesn’t want Keegan and Boo to know about the missing videos so to buy time until they’re recovered, Sally institutes a screen-free Christmas for her family while secretly searching for the tapes. After she connects with Damon at his uncle’s antique store, he joins the hunt and the two grow closer. Keegan and Boo soon discover the joys of unplugging and spending quality time with their grandparents, who also come around and embrace the experiment after begrudgingly agreeing. With every lead exhausted, Sally is forced to admit the videos may be gone forever. As the fate of the tapes is in flux, the family learns the importance of cherishing old memories and creating new ones.

"My Christmas Cowboy"Stars: Amy Acker, Luke MacfarlaneLogline: Meg (Acker) set aside her newscaster aspirations after a disastrous audition experience in college and has been happy as a news producer in her small town of Fern, Texas. Billy Kane (Macfarlane), her former college crush and audition partner, is a well-known celebrity host in Hollywood on the brink of losing his career after an on-camera gaffe. At the advice of his publicist, Billy begrudgingly returns to Texas to lay low and spend the holidays with his sister (Canning) and her family. When Meg and Billy cross paths he’s happy to see her but her feelings are on the frostier side – she’s still upset he took advantage of her failed audition to get the gig himself. Meg finds herself seeing Billy more than she’d like since his nephew Graham (Isaiah Haegert) is in the horse therapy program her dad runs at their ranch. With their annual Reindeer Roundup holiday event coming up Meg’s dad gets sidelined after an injury. Her dad enlists Billy to serve as its host, much to Meg’s chagrin. With the Reindeer Roundup just days away, Meg teaches Billy basic riding and roping skills to get him ready for his hosting duties. In the process, they slowly reconnect and Meg sees there’s more to him than Hollywood glitz. As their connection grows, each of them helps give the other the courage to step outside their comfort zones and find new joy – and possibly love – in unexpected ways.

"The Nights Before Christmas"Stars: Tyler Hynes, Laci J MaileyLogline: One Christmas Eve Marty (Hynes), whose life is in a bit of a rut, finds himself wishing he had more time. Thanks to some holiday magic, he awakes the next morning to discover it’s Christmas Eve – again. Confused at first, Marty learns to embrace his new normal and begins to truly appreciate the sights, sounds and people of New York City that previously went unnoticed. With this gift of time, he expands his world by learning how to play a new instrument, picking up new languages and reading…every single book. But when Marty meets Chloe (Mailey), a newly out-of-work journalist having a tough day, he falls hard for her. The only problem is that when the morning of December 24 comes once again, she doesn’t know who he is. As the Christmas Eves continue to repeat themselves, Marty makes it his mission to win her over and, in the process, figure out what he needs to do to finally make his way to Christmas Day – hopefully with Chloe by his side.

"Mistletoe and Mimosas"Stars: Tamera Mowry-Housley, Kristoffer Polaha, Jennifer RobertsonLogline: Claire Bennett (Mowry-Housley) is a successful business consultant in Manhattan who unexpectedly inherits her beloved Uncle Lou’s Christmas-themed bar, The Tipsy Reindeer, in upstate New York. When she returns, Claire discovers the bar comes with high debt – her Uncle Lou was overly generous to people in town while the booming business of Algorithm, an upscale and trendy new club, added insult to injury. She intends to turn things around before Christmas and sell to someone who will preserve her uncle’s legacy and then return to her life in the city. Claire meets Zach (Polaha), Algorithm’s part owner and manager, who tells her they want to buy The Tipsy Reindeer so they can expand. Claire bristles at the proposition and they agree to face off in a 12 Days of Christmas-inspired series of festive events to see who can bring in the most business – if Claire wins, Zach will use his contacts to find the right buyer but if Zach emerges victorious, Claire agrees to consider Algorithm’s offer. As they compete over the course of the 12 days their attraction is undeniable. Rivalry leads to romance and the two are faced with figuring out how their shifting priorities might somehow lead them down the same road, together.

"Our Holiday Playbook"Stars: Taylor Cole, Charles Michael Davis.Logline: When Lexi Bell (Cole) returns home for the holidays, she faces a beloved family tradition she’d rather avoid: the fiercely competitive Bell Bowl, an annual Christmas flag football showdown between her father and uncle that has fueled decades of sibling rivalry. But when an injury sidelines her brother-in-law it looks like Lexi’s family’s losing streak will remain unbroken. To give them a fighting chance, she strikes a deal with Eddie (Davis), a former local football star-turned teacher – Lexi will use her baking know-how to help Eddie best his brother in their annual bake-off if he’ll pose as her boyfriend and meet the “eligibility requirement” to play on their team. As they navigate each other’s festive family gatherings, traditions and celebrations, what started as a transactional partnership begins to become something more as Lexi and Eddie find themselves feeling less and less like their romantic relationship is just pretend. As the two clans battle it out on the field, regardless of who takes home the trophy Lexi may have already won at love.

"Christmas in Blue Dog Valley"Stars: Erin Cahill, Andrew WalkerLogline: On-set veterinarian Goldie MacKenzie (Cahill) leaves the glamour of Hollywood behind to buy a family-run veterinary clinic in tight-knit Blue Dog Valley, arriving just in time for the town’s cherished Christmas season. When Dr. Gable, the clinic’s longtime owner, unexpectedly ends up out of town, Goldie is hosted by his handsome son Cohen (Walker), the black sheep of the family because he decided to forego their expectation of becoming a vet. Cohen and Goldie get off on the wrong foot, but when the folks of Blue Dog Valley cold shoulder “the newcomer,” Cohen teams up with Goldie to win over even the frostiest of community members. Goldie is also aided by the mysterious canine she dubs Blue whose spontaneous appearances always seem to guide Goldie to exactly where she needs to be. As Goldie works hard to prove herself to the townspeople when furry and Christmas crises arise, she finds herself pulled towards the very heart of her new-found home...and a certain black sheep.

"Double Booked for the Holidays"Stars: Rachael Leigh Cook, Owain Yeoman, Stephen HaganLogline: There’s only one thing identical twins, quiet and bookish Abigail (Cook) and globe-trotting event planner Charlie (Cook), agree on is that this first Christmas without their mom will be difficult. When they unexpectedly get a last-minute chance to travel to Wales and spend a week running the Story Shoppe, an AirBnb/bookshop in Hay-on-Wye, they jump at the opportunity. Abigail is particularly excited, given the town’s role as the backdrop of the bestselling Winterton Chronicles, her all-time favorite Regency holiday romances. Upon arrival, Abigail dives into setting up the bookshop’s window display with help from the friendly next-door barista, Tom (Yeoman), who is also a fan of the Winterton Chronicles. Meanwhile, Charlie meets the dashing Lord Rhys (Hagan), the great-nephew of Evelyn Calon, who wrote the book series. Abigail is charmed by a series of thoughtful Christmas ornaments she assumes are from Rhys (but are actually from Tom), while Charlie and Rhys grow closer as they help plan the Winterton Ball at Rhys’ castle. Mistaken identities lead to a series of merry mix-ups as Rhys and Tom woo the sisters, unaware they are twins. On the night of the ball, however, the sisters’ double secret is discovered. As the truth is unwrapped, the crisscrossed lovers discover that the perfect holiday happy ending isn’t always by the book.

"Christmas Delivered"Stars: Autumn Reeser, Wes BrownLogline: Determined to unwind from the stresses and loneliness of her everyday life, Kimberly Carr (Reeser) travels to Canada to spend Christmas with her grandmother, JoJo (Linda Darlow), at her beautiful, cozy farmhouse. Kimberly's plans for a restorative holiday are turned upside down when she crosses paths with Ben Chambers (Brown), owner of a local tree farm and new Christmas tree delivery app called TreeBen. Ben's a dreamer who never looks before he leaps while Kimberly is methodical and lives her life based on practicality – the two couldn't be more different. But when Ben’s app is plagued by an onslaught of issues, Kimberly uses her tech expertise to help him out and ensure that no one in town is deprived of a Christmas tree...even though she isn’t convinced of the need for the app in such a small town. As they team up to deliver trees in his red truck, Kimberly and Ben discover they may have more in common than they realized. In the process, Kimberly begins to question if she’s truly happy with her life or if she’s ready for a change and – just maybe – ready for romance.

"The Christmas Eve Feast"*Premieres 6pm ET/PTStars: Daniella Monet, Kevin McGarryLogline: Silvana “Silvy” Gianetti (Monet) is disillusioned with her job as the Executive Chef at a swanky restaurant in New York. Growing up in a large and loving Italian-American family, Silvy is drawn to the food and comfort of her home. When her beloved Nonna suffers a minor wrist injury, Silvy is called back home to Boston’s Italian North End to prepare the family’s beloved “Feast of the Seven Fishes” Christmas Eve dinner. As she preps for the big feast, her family is joined by Ethan (McGarry), a photographer who is documenting different family traditions around town and who’s become close to her Nonna. After a rocky start with Ethan, things begin to heat up as Silvy grows to appreciate the heart and soul he puts into capturing the magic of the little moments and a romance could be simmering. Every day leading up to Christmas Eve, Silvy gathers in the kitchen with her Nonna, mom and aunt to prepare the pasta, struffoli and other Italian classics near and dear to Silvy’s heart. This special family time reminds her of the kind of cooking that truly brings her joy and leads Silvy to rethink where she belongs and gets a clear picture of who should be by her side.

"Return to Santa"Stars: Paul Campbell, Rachel BostonLogline: Hopeful and dreamy eight-year-old Jake (Campbell) writes a letter to Santa with all his most fantastical wishes. But when the letter gets lost in the North Pole, young Jake wakes up disappointed, and no longer a believer. Decades later Santa discovers the misplaced letter and immediately sets out to make things right. Now an adult, Jake’s life is about to get turned upside down when the appearance of his childhood wishes clash with his practical life. All while his childhood best friend Julie (Boston) rather unexpectedly moved back to town. As Santa continues to check off Jake’s list, Jake and Julie combine forces to anticipate each new wishes’ chaotic consequences, all while growing closer to each other – and possibly leading Jake closer to his most important childhood dream.

"The Most Wonderful Secret"*Premieres 6pm ET/PTStars: Tammin Sursok, Peter PorteLogline: Every Christmas, a small town honors the memory of a beloved teacher who once spread joy through her “Secret Norma” gifts each holiday by creating a whimsical and heartfelt scavenger hunt for one worthy recipient. When burned-out art teacher Vanessa (Sursok) visits her widowed brother and niece Esther for the holidays, she is surprised to be chosen as the next “Secret Norma” recipient. Hoping to bring Esther some Christmas magic, Vanessa decides to help revive the town’s holiday block party. Her handsome electrician neighbor Spencer (Porte) offers help with the preparations if Vanessa will help him sell his mother Norma’s house. As Vanessa solves the riddles of “Secret Norma” and plans the block party, her passion for teaching art begins to spark along with her feelings for the charming electrician next door.

"Holiday Ever After: A Disney World Wish Come True"Stars: Lacey Chabert, Travis Van Winkle, Richard Kind, Christy Carlson Romano, Bryce Durfee, Taegen Burns, Asher AlexanderLogline: Lindsey (Lacey Chabert) and her extended family head to Walt Disney World to spend a magical Christmas together. But the dream of a jolly holiday gets quickly dashed when Lindsey discovers her room is next door to Philip (Travis Van Winkle), a disastrous first date she recently had, who’s also there on a family trip. As Lindsey and Philip’s paths cross throughout their stay, the frost starts to thaw as they learn they’re not so different from each other after all. Thanks to some Walt Disney World magic, the holiday wish Lindsey made in Cinderella Fountain just might turn their rivalry into romance.

"Eight Nights for Love"*Premieres 6pm ET/PTStars: Hunter King, Dan JeannotteLogline: Hannah (King), who works for a large auction house in New York City, is excited for her best friend Ethan (Jeannotte) to return home for a visit during Hannukah and is looking forward to some much-needed time off from work That plan is short lived when Ethan shares the news that he’s convinced the daughter of his wealthy boss to use Hannah’s auction house to sell their family’s collection of Judaica with the condition that Hannah handles the sale. Complicating her holiday further, she meets the mysterious Pearl (Felicia Shulman), who gifts her with an antique menorah that is anything but ordinary as it takes her back to a different times of her life each night of Hanukkah, with Pearl as her guide. This front row seat past moments – including some that involve Ethan – leads Hannah to reflect, break out of her comfort zone and overcome her fear of failure. Thanks to her trips through the past, and as she and Ethan spend time together in the present Hannah realizes she has feelings for him she never acknowledged. Through this journey, Hannah makes some bold decisions about her life – and love – that are sure to make this Hanukkah one to remember.

"Miles to Christmas"Stars: Ashley Williams, Steve Lund, Alison SweeneyLogline: When an early snowstorm sweeps through the Midwest, punctual, straight-laced “suit” Cassidy Fields (Williams) is forced to hitch a ride with free spirited, music loving Johanna “Jo” Woods (Sweeney) in her bother Chase’s (Lund) 18-wheeler to the nearest airport to catch another flight. However, when Jo’s flight successfully takes off and Cassidy’s is cancelled again at the last minute, she joins Chase on the road back to Tennessee from Chicago to make it home in time to spend Christmas with her father. Quickly, Cassidy and Chase’s connection begins to spark. Through losing the car keys, stopping to partake in a Mrs. Claus parade and a surprise run-in with Jo, whose plane got grounded mid-flight due to weather, Cassidy builds bonds with both siblings as they all challenge one another’s life philosophies. As the trio pushes past every obstacle, they work to embrace their differences and find that the fastest way home is when they lean on one another for help.

"The Snowflake Effect"Stars: Heather Hemmens, Mark GhaniméLogline: When driven corporate attorney Tanya (Hemmens) rushes into a charming gift shop searching for a last-minute White Elephant gift, she crosses paths with Jason (Ghanimé), a handsome, laid-back clerk. Their brief encounter leads Tanya to purchase a beautiful antique glass snowflake which, unbeknownst to her or Jason, is a good luck charm that carries a generations-old Christmas tradition. However, since the ornament is entered into a holiday gift exchange rather than gifted with proper intention, Tanya suddenly finds herself on the receiving end of everyone else’s misfortune. After Jason’s Aunt Coco (Jayne Eastwood) explains the snowflake’s magical lore, Tanya reluctantly teams up with Jason to track down the snowflake as it makes its way from one recipient to the next across Chicago before Christmas Day or she’ll be stuck with bad luck until next Christmas. Along the way, the pair is swept into festive holiday adventures, unexpected encounters and a journey that challenges Tanya’s carefully structured life. As they race against the clock to undo the snowflake’s magic, Tanya and Jason’s relationship turns into something more and they may find that their biggest stroke of luck was meeting each other.

"A Grand Biltmore Christmas" Stars: Holland Roden, Niall Matter, Andie MacDowell, James Trevena, Jonathan Frakes, Rachel Boston, Wes Brown.Logline: As Biltmore House opens for the first time on Christmas Eve 1895, 13-year-old Elizabeth and her family are holiday guests. When she notices Michael, a fellow teen caught trespassing by the staff, Elizabeth comes to his rescue by claiming to know him, much to his relief. The two share an instant connection and set out to explore Biltmore but Michael inexplicably vanishes. Twenty years later, Elizabeth (Roden) is spending Christmas at Biltmore and this time is accompanied by James (Trevena), a suitor her Aunt Maysilee (MacDowell), is keen for her to wed. When a stranger asks Elizabeth to dance at the Christmas gala she’s shocked to discover it’s Michael (Matter). Thrilled to reunite with her friend, she throws herself into his arms. But the world around her changes in an instant when Elizabeth is transported into the modern world with Michael, a tourist from the present day who had traveled to the past 20 years prior with the help of a magical hourglass in Biltmore’s library. Now, Elizabeth and Michael must find a way to send her back to her time, while not arousing the suspicion of Michael’s mother and sister during their family vacation. As Elizabeth experiences life and Christmas in the 21st century, she and Michael become close. When the time comes for her to return to 1915, Elizabeth must decide whether she’ll resume the life that’s been chosen for her or if her heart will lead her down a new path in the present.SUNDAY, DEC. 6

"An Angel in My Stocking"Stars: Fionna Gubelmann, Marco Grazzini, Siobhan Williams, Nancy Robertson Logline: Amanda (Gubelmann) and Jack (Grazzini) had a whirlwind romance and got married after knowing each other for only three months. Their first – and only – Christmas together was calamitous and was the beginning of the end to their brief marriage. Three years post-divorce and still harboring an aversion to the holiday, Amanda is heading to Vermont with her sister Lucy (Williams) to enjoy an un-Christmasy getaway…and finds that Jack is on their flight. En route, Amanda meets Margaret (Kane), a quirky traveler who disappears without a trace and without being seen by anyone else, leaving Amanda mystified. Bad weather diverts the plane to the remote town of Pinecone Lake, leaving Amanda with the last person she wants to be stranded with – Jack. Shortly after arrival, Margaret inexplicably reappears and convinces a confused Amanda that she is in fact her guardian angel and has been her entire life. As the days leading to Christmas pass by, Amanda slowly begins to feel connected to the community and, with Margaret’s guidance, sees beyond past circumstances and follows her heart to where – and with whom – she truly belongs.

"Christmas in Canterbury"Stars: Jessy Schram, Will KempLogline: Rose (Schram) arrives in Canterbury, England eager to spend the holidays with her childhood friend Asha (Sohm Kapila) as she leaves behind her hometown of Vienna, OH following the passing of her beloved Grandma Bud. Having first met in a children’s choir they went on to pursue careers as choir masters. As Rose arrives Asha is put on bed rest in the final days of her pregnancy. Rose steps in when the headmistress offers her the job…not realizing there was confusion over which Vienna children’s choir she worked with. Rose’s “glass half full” attitude is tested when she crosses paths with Harrison (Kemp), the traditionalist boys’ choir master who has an unwavering allegiance to history and precedents. The boys’ choir always performs at the annual Christmas Eve concert in Canterbury Cathedral but Rose questions why the girls don’t have the opportunity. When the school’s headmistress decides the two choirs should compete against each other for the honor, they get to work to prepare their students. Along the way, their rivalry sparks a romance and these two seemingly opposites from opposite sides of the pond discover they may not be so different after all.

"Snow Globe Town"Stars: Kimberley Sustad, Scott Michael FosterLogline: Inspired by Brad Paisley’s song “Snow Globe Town,” this heartfelt holiday romance follows Emily Church (Sustad), who joins her sister Zoe and Zoe’s longtime boyfriend on a Christmas getaway to Pine Grove, the town famously known as the Christmas Proposal Capital of America. Expecting to help capture a photos of Zoe’s perfect engagement moment as is their family’s tradition, Emily instead finds herself unexpectedly sidelined by the town’s couples-only traditions and paired with Bert Baxter (Foster), a skeptical journalist researching the celebrated romantic legacy inspired by his grandfather. As Emily quietly works behind the scenes to help Zoe’s proposal plans come together, she and Bert are drawn into the town’s festive traditions, holiday competitions and Christmas celebrations. Along the way they discover a shared outlook on love and life that challenges both of their expectations. As old assumptions are tested and new possibilities emerge, Pine Grove reminds them that love, family and the spirit of Christmas often arrive in the most unexpected ways.

"Noelle Nomads"Stars: Benjamin Ayres, Torrey DeVitto, Holland Roden.Logline: Joseph has to deliver a gift from his late father to a campground, but things go wrong at every turn. With the help of Nora, he learns to embrace nature and its beauty.

"Barking All the Way"Stars: Ian Harding, Tori AndersonLogline: Billie (Anderson) is a workaholic realtor who heads home for Christmas but her journey is derailed after loveable, but chaotic canine named Yappy almost causes her car to crash. After talking to Yappy’s owner, the mysterious, yet oddly familiar Mrs. C, Billie agrees to watch Yappy while she visits her grandchildren for the holidays. Yappy ends up playing the role of matchmaker and new best friend, pulling Billie towards her traveling contractor ex-boyfriend from high school, Hutch (Harding). Eager to move on she’s determined to leave Hutch in the past, but when her mother hires him to work on their shed, she finds herself spending more time with him than she ever expected. As the holidays draw closer, Billie begins to question whether chasing her dream of becoming her firm’s number one seller is truly what she wants. When the mysterious Mrs. C leaves her cabin for Billie and Hutch to breathe new life into, her answer may come sooner than expected.

"Save the Date for Christmas" Stars: Jonathan Bennett, Italia RicciLogline: Susie (Ricci) has checked out on dating while Alec (Benett) is a hopeless romantic – these longtime friends have both struck out in the love department after failing to meet the right man. After being each other's plus one to what feels like the twentieth wedding this year, they vow to take a break from attending weddings and looking for their respective prince charming. That break doesn’t last long as next day Susie's sister announces a last-minute Christmas wedding…and Susie convinces Alec to tag along. The objective for the week? Survive as the two lone, single people and avoid family matchmaking. Over time, the Christmas wedding duties and time with family during the holidays force these two best friends to forge a new appreciation for love and marriage. Susie finds herself turning over a new leaf in pursuing romance while Alec discovers love can walk into your life when you least expect it.

#3534. These Sony ANC Headphones Are on Sale for $128 Right Now

It's hard to convince yourself to spend nearly half a grand on premium headphones, like the Sony WH-1000XM6, even if you consider yourself an audiophile. Not everyone can afford those prices, which is why the budget, mid-tier, and premium tiers exist. While the premium 1000XM6 headphones are over three times the price of the mid-tier Sony WH-CH730N, they're not three times as good. The Sony WH-CH730N are $128 (originally $179) right now, the lowest price they've ever been according to price-tracking tools, and they offer an amazing value for your money.

It's pretty impressive what $128 in headphones gets you in 2026. The CH730N uses the same Sony Connect app as the premium headphones; as a result, you get a 10-band slider on the EQ menu, a battery care feature that extends the longevity of your battery life, 50 hours of juice, ANC, Ambient Sound (transparency mode), Multipoint to connect to two devices at once, and Bluetooth 6.0. The Adaptive Sound Control feature can detect your activity (walking, sitting down, loud environment, etc.) and automatically switch the level of ANC and transparency to make your experience as comfortable and seamless as possible.

The microphones are decent and use a feature to isolate your voice in noisy environments. I love that there's an AUX connection to give you the option, which seems to be coming back with newer headphones. The design is light and will feel like plastic, but they are comfortable to wear for long sessions. If you're looking to maximize the quality of headphones you can get for your money, the Sony WH-CH730N offer a pretty compelling option at $128.

#3533. The Subpoenas Are Coming, the Subpoenas Are Coming: Tech Execs Brace for Congressional Crackdown, Say Lobbyists

On Thursday, I was on the phone with a source when he suddenly sounded like he’d gotten the wind knocked out of him. We were in the middle of talking about antitrust policy when he exhaled and said, “Wow. Worst one-day destruction of value in history. Just got the Wall Street Journal alert.”

The tech world—and the markets built on top of it—is still figuring out how to feel about last week’s momentous Democratic midterm sweep. My Republican sources, unsurprisingly, reported that the vibes in their ranks are “horrendous.” Anyone who works with data centers is just about ready to throw in the towel on planet Earth and take their infrastructure efforts to space, with voters having opposed data center construction via 40 different ballot measures. And then there’s the more general rebuke of the future the tech industry is building, and the possible implications for an economy that’s increasingly come to revolve around it.

Indeed, it seems that the debate over AI has really, truly broken through to the mainstream this year: According to an NBC exit poll, 56% of voters called AI and data centers a “crucial or major factor” in their votes for Congress. Amid the free-for-all of President Trump’s first two years back in office, AI companies have been allowed to develop their technology largely free of regulatory oversight, but they may now be forced to pump the brakes.

In a lengthy interview with Ross Douthat on CBS’s 60 Minutes, Trump said he was open to working with Democrats to implement some AI guardrails. Still, no one I spoke to this week told me they expect to see sweeping AI legislation—unless, as two different tech Democrats suggested, there is an AI-caused catastrophe that “scares the shit out of us.”

Democratic Senators like Bernie Sanders and Elizabeth Warren have already begun making plans to investigate tech corporations.

In the absence of such an event, “we expect [new AI laws] to be narrow and bipartisan. Child safety, AI agent liability, and predeployment testing, for example, all have Republican cosponsors,” said Christina Ho, an executive at the financial auditing firm Oath Verified.

Meanwhile, even more explicitly MAGA-coded industries could see more concrete crackdowns. Those in “the crypto world,” who spent the first year of Trump 2.0 flying high, now “realize they’re screwed,” said an executive at a conservative think tank—especially as famed crypto critic Sherrod Brown makes his big return to the Senate with, as one Democratic strategist put it, an “axe to grind.”

Defense-tech founders and investors may also find themselves toning down their rhetoric as the testosterone-fueled “Department of War” era comes to an end with the possible impeachment of Secretary Pete Hegseth. In recent years, “dual use” has become a bit of a “dirty word,” said Cody Huggins, a partner at Scout Ventures. He suspects that promoting the commercial applications of military technologies, from satellites to drones, “will come back to be a little bit more sexy than it has been.”

Perhaps the biggest winners of the post-midterms period will be the DC law firms brought on to help manage the flood of subpoenas promised by politicians like Bernie Sanders and Elizabeth Warren. “AI executives might be called to testify,” said Ho, adding, “Companies would be wise to prepare their executives for the witness table before they prepare for any new laws.”

A Democratic tech lobbyist told me that one of his clients has already received a list of questions from a congressional committee. “They’re not waiting to have gavels,” he said.

Luther Lowe, the head of public policy at the start-up accelerator Y Combinator, is hoping to see a return to the antitrust revolution once promised by former FTC chair Lina Khan. “I think some of that stuff could come back online,” he said, referring to antitrust legislation that then Senate majority leader Chuck Schumer declined to bring to a vote in 2022.

In the future, tech executives who went all in on MAGA (right after going all in on woke) may want to consider some age-old advice: just be yourself. “Companies need to stop thinking about political outcomes as permanent conditions. Regulations change, governments change, and priorities change. That’s not new,” said Andrew Peek, CEO of the investing platform Tilt. “What’s different now is the sheer amount of money being committed to technologies whose economics are still evolving. If your entire strategy only works under one political scenario, that’s a pretty big risk to be taking.”

Still, there was one midterm fight in which the tech world definitively won out: the one over Proposition 40, or California’s so-called billionaire tax, which was defeated. Some suspect that the hundreds of millions of dollars spent by Silicon Valley billionaires to defeat the measure could backfire. “There’s a growing wave of anger and resentment from the working class that is coming for them,” said the Democratic strategist. The irony of spending so much money to fight the tax, he said, is that if it had passed, it could have “temporarily removed some of the pressure in the pressure cooker.” All that money having been spent to shut down the tax, he warned, “is gonna make things much worse.”

#3532. This Samsung 32-Inch OLED Gaming Monitor Is $300 Off Right Now

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. Previously, she spent a year teaching English at the junior high level.An avid reader since childhood, Pradershika's idea of extreme sports is staying up to read “just one more chapter.” She lives in India.

Amazon currently has the 32-inch Samsung Odyssey OLED G8 (G80SH) for $999.99, down from $1,299.99, and price trackers show that this is its lowest price so far. This is the newer 4K OLED model, not Samsung’s similarly named G80HS, which is a 6K IPS variant, and it makes the most sense for someone who wants one screen for both high-end gaming and everyday desktop use without moving to a larger ultrawide.

Its 4K QD-OLED panel runs at 240Hz, which gives the G80SH enough speed for competitive shooters and racing games while still keeping slower, more cinematic games looking sharp. You will need a powerful PC to get anywhere close to 4K at 240Hz, but the monitor is at least equipped for newer graphics hardware with DisplayPort 2.1 and HDMI 2.1. It also has USB-C with up to 98W of power delivery, so if this monitor doubles as a work setup, a compatible laptop can send video and charge over the same cable instead of adding another wire to your desk. FreeSync Premium Pro and G-SYNC compatibility should also help keep tearing under control, though OLED monitors can still show visible VRR flicker in darker scenes when frame pacing is inconsistent.

The bigger visual difference, though, shows up in darker games and HDR content, where blacks stay properly black and bright effects stand out without the blooming you often see on LCD monitors. That said, QD-OLED does have its own drawbacks, since blacks can take on a purplish tint in a brightly lit room, while burn-in remains a long-term concern—though Samsung does include active cooling and several screen-protection features to reduce uneven wear and says burn-in from normal use is covered under warranty. If you mostly play at lower frame rates or do not care much about OLED contrast, this is probably more monitor than you need, but for someone with the graphics hardware to take advantage of 4K at 240Hz, this discount makes the G80SH much easier to justify.

The Blade Runner saga is set to continue amid the 2026 TV schedule, thanks to an upcoming limited series. Blade Runner 2099 presents the next chapter in this science-fiction-infused tale of humans and replicants and puts new protagonists at the forefront. Given what’s come before, it’s only natural to wonder whether the show has direct connections to Ridley Scott’s original 1982 film and Denis Villeneuve’s 2017 sequel, 2049. Well, the showrunner is now shedding some light on that front.

If it weren’t already clear due to the title, 2099 picks up fifty years after the events of the critically acclaimed Blade Runner 2049. That film left quite a few plot threads on the table, including the revelation that the late Eldon Tyrell gave replicants the ability to reproduce. Heading up the new show is Silka Luisa, who is a longtime fan of the franchise. Luisa recently spoke with SFX Magazine on CinemaBlend and was asked if events from 2049 would come into play. With that, she gave a very clear answer:

No, [Blade Runner 2049] is not directly connected to the show. What was an important early mandate was that audiences could come to the show not having seen the films, and this could stand alone. This could be an introduction to the world of Blade Runner, and it wouldn’t be dependent on you having watched 2049, you having watched the first Blade Runner. In that sense, we had to divorce ourselves from the narrative.

Why Edward James Olmos Says He Owes His Battlestar Galactica Legacy To Blade Runner

Some fans may be a tad disappointed to learn that replicant reproduction won’t be expanded upon during the events of the show. Yet Luisa’s “mandate” does indeed make a lot of sense. What she and her collaborators ultimately want is a show that fits snugly into the continuity but also doesn’t require watching the movies. (Of course, both of those films are excellent and deserve to be watched regardless.) In short, the Shining Girls creator is promising a series that works on its own, and that could do away with any trepidation newcomers may have about jumping in.

Blade Runner 2099 takes viewers to a Los Angeles that’s now fully controlled by replicants, and humans must essentially live within the lower levels of society. At the center of the story is Olwen, a Replicant Blade Runner (played by Michelle Yeoh) who is only days away from dying. She is eventually partnered with Marion Jessop to take on a case. However, unbeknownst to Olwen, “Marion” is actually a human named Cora (Hunter Schafer), who is only masquerading as a Replicant to achieve her own goals.

Per what’s been shared thus far, Yeoh and Schafer forged a strong bond on set not unlike Harrison Ford and Ryan Gosling did while making 2049. However, as far as we know, Yeoh didn’t accidentally punch Schafer in the face like Ford did to Gosling. In fact, Yeoh was protective of her co-star amid production and, in a truly mom-coded move, she even bought Schafer a baby helmet.

The trailers for 2099 would suggest that such headgear was necessary, because a lot of intense moments have been teased thus far. Although fans won’t see any direct links to the Blade Runner films, Silka Luisa is aiming to dish out the action-infused thrills, heightened visuals and deep themes that have long permeated this franchise.

Check out Blade Runner 2099 when all eight episodes are released for Prime Video subscription holders on November 25. In the meantime, anyone who’s curious can stream the original movie for free on Pluto TV and check out 2049 on Prime as well.
